Microsoft's SideWinder Strategic Commander was a failed attempt to reimagine RTS controls. 23 years later, why are some players still using it?

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1509 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rockpapershotgun

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that PC players have been conditioned for decades to accept the keyboard-and-mouse setup for RTS games.
  • In a recent development, unveiled on March 1st 2000 at Microsoft's Gamestock event, the Strategic Commander was one of three additions to their SideWinder line, with a scheduled release that October at a pricey $64.95.
  • Microsoft, all the while, were taking notes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that PC players have been conditioned for decades to accept the keyboard-and-mouse setup for RTS games. One hand has to handle movement and commands through a keyboard, while the other points, drags, and selects with a mouse. Peripheral makers have, usually with the addition of more buttons, made many minor variations to this time-honored arrangement, but there's only ever been one real attempt to rethink it entirely for the PC: the Microsoft SideWinder Strategic Commander.

In a recent development, unveiled on March 1st 2000 at Microsoft's Gamestock event, the Strategic Commander was one of three additions to their SideWinder line, with a scheduled release that October at a pricey $64.95. At E3 later that May, Microsoft demonstrated the Strategic Commander for the first time with SimCity 3000, while promoting its potential for other such games as Diablo II, Warcraft III, and Baldur's Gate II. This was all taking place during the so-called 'Golden Age of Real-Time Strategy Games,' which spanned roughly from the mid-1990s to the mid-2000s. It was when the RTS genre was at the peak of its mainstream popularity, and we fans were devoted to mastering its intricacies in any way we could to have a competitive edge.

Microsoft, all the while, were taking notes. "The team conceived the Strategic Commander in the late 1990s," Carl Ledbetter - then Industrial Design Manager for Microsoft's PC Hardware Group, now Head of Design for Xbox Devices - recalls to me. "As RTS games grew in popularity, we saw an interesting opportunity to design a upcoming physical interface around a new interaction model. The idea was for it to be used left-handed in concert with right-hand PC desktop mouse control. We wanted to enable players to perform faster with more fluidity, comfort, optimised control placement for multiple hand sizes, simplicity of set-up, and ease of programming.".

Industry observers note that for Ledbetter and co. to realise this ambition, the Strategic Commander was designed as a unique combination of mouse, joystick, and gamepad. To manage the increasing complexities of the RTS games of the day, it came equipped with six programmable buttons, three shift buttons, and a three-position profile switch. Back then, these atypical features provided an unprecedented 72 possible key combinations across various configurations, all at the tip of our stubby little fingers. Better yet, it allowed us to toggle between three pre-configured profiles at a time, so that we could switch up our configurations on the fly depending on which stage of an RTS match we were in.

Industry observers note that on release, contemporary reviewers acknowledged its originality, with critics like ActiveWin's Julien Jay describing it as "probably the most innovative (with the GameVoice) and revolutionary" peripheral designed specifically for strategy players. Others, like Neoseeker's Arnel Lim, suggested that it might’ve gone overboard with its customisation options, saying "you won't use anywhere close to all of them," in reference to the controller's programmable key combinations. Either way, the Strategic Commander failed to supplant conventional peripherals in the hands of most RTS players, and it was discontinued in 2003. As was the rest of the original SideWinder line, owing to declining sales and the industry-wide shift toward standard M+K setups for all PC games and genres.

However, unlike so many of its Microsoft-made siblings, this was not the end for the Strategic Commander. Niche as it was, it went on to enjoy a surprisingly long post-shelf life, one that was stretched out by a dedicated cult following - and that continues to this day. But why? Why, after all these years, is this forgotten peripheral from a discontinued line maintaining such a enthusiastic fanbase, years after the industry around it had written it off as a failure?

Industry observers note that the answer lies in software and OS compatibility, as much as the hardware's own appeal. Andreas Weis was the developer of one of the first unofficial patches for the Strategic Commander, allowing players to keep on using it even after the original software stopped being compatible with newer versions the Windows. By that point, the device was a decade old, and well into 'official' obsolescence, yet Weis still answered the call of the Strategic Commander's righteously frustrated - if numerically few - fans. "There was a lot of interest back in the early 2010s in software patches to keep the Strategic Commander functional when the original software for the Strategic Commander stopped working," he explains. "Consumers were asking around on internet forums about how to get it to work on Windows 7 and Vista machines. Since I was studying computer science at the time, I was quite interested in reverse-engineering, and I hacked together a simple tool that would cover my use cases for the device.".

In the years that followed, other patches were released to keep the Strategic Commander operational, the most notable of which was Philip Merwarth’s Strategic Engine software in 2013. Unfortunately, they weren’t open-source. Worse was that the protocol for programming the Strategic Commander wasn’t documented anywhere online in a way that was accessible for users. This is why Weis realized that he could make a unique contribution.

"I polished my old prototype code for the Strategic Commander software patch and released it as a library, so that other people could use it to write their own applications for programming the tool," he indicates. "As for me, I released one application that made use of the library publicly, the vJoy feeder application, which allows the device to be used with games that support joystick inputs." Curiously, Weis, by this time and like many others, had found other applications for a device with such a specific selling point, and even continues to use the Strategic Commander sparingly in 2026.

"The production quality of Microsoft hardware at the time was just top-notch, and I love the design of the old SideWinder devices, which is why I did not just throw the thing out when the software stopped working," he tells me. "It was worth keeping around to find newly introduced uses for it over the years, and I eventually realized that it makes quite a nice addition to a HOTAS (Hands-On Throttle And Stick) setup, where I could put actions that aren’t time-critical and don't fit well on the throttle on the Strategic Commander instead. For example, when I’m playing Elite Dangerous in VR, I’d put actions like deploying the landing gear on the Strategic Commander to free up buttons on the throttle for actions that were more relevant for combat.".

Sources indicate that when looking back at the history of Microsoft’s SideWinder line, it’s easy to call the Strategic Commander a failed experiment, given the fact that most of us are still using the same standard mouse-and-keyboard setup to play RTS games. However, the central premise behind its design philosophy was that the interface between a player and a game could be redesigned to cater to specific genre quirks, and decades following its release, it’s still maintained a coalition of loyal customers: some RTS players who believed the Strategic Commander really pulled it off, and those found other uses for the device in other flavours of PC game. And with the concern of modern compatibility, a roadblock for so much retro hardware, bypassed by homemade patches, both camps can continue twisting and clicking their Strategic Commanders unimpeded.

All the same, I wonder if it might have basked in more conventional success, had Microsoft made more forward-thinking decisions. The Strategic Commander has proven over the years that its unprecedented customisation had applications far beyond what Ledbetter’s team had envisioned, and once the popularity of RTS games settled down, other, similar click-heavy subgenres like MOBAs and Real-Time Tactics got substantial as well. Would a more officially maintained, potentially refined Strategic Commander model have served those crowds? I think it might. The narrow focus on RTS games may have also hurt the device's since-demonstrated broader appeal; if Microsoft had fully capitalised on this customisation selling point by communicating its benefits to everyone, not just those playing the single most popular PC genre at the time, it could have provided the blueprint for a proper, long-lived alternative to controllers, mice, and keyboards.

Recent findings suggest that alas, gaming history is littered with revolutionary peripherals that failed to actually revolutionise the industry surrounding them. The Strategic Commander is no different, but for the fact that it’s had this surprisingly long post-shelf life - and, as a result, the opportunity for insight into what could have been done to salvage the its failures. Still, that unexpected longevity can provide come comfort to the Strategic Commander's creators, as well as its lingering owners.

In a recent development, "I think the design made sense for its time, especially with the rising popularity of RTS games," Ledbetter reflects. "Looking back, I would have liked more time to test and refine the Strategic Commander. I’m proud of what we brought to market, and I’m glad to know that it remains beloved by many players to this day.".

In a recent development, the Lord of the Rings: The Hunt for Gollum has wrapped filming, but we're still yet to see a proper first look at our favorite characters returning. However, that hasn't stopped fake images of the movie circulating online, which Frodo star Elijah Wood has been quick to point out.

Recent findings suggest that an online publication posted on Twitter what it called the "first look behind the scenes images" of the upcoming film. This featured mock-ups of Lee Pace's return as Thranduil, Ian McKellen back as Gandalf the Grey, and Wood as Frodo Baggins, as well as what it branded as the first look at Jamie Dornan as Aragorn and Anya Taylor-Joy as Seren.

It's pretty clear they are AI-mock-ups as they feature strange, uncanny details like changing coffee cup sizes and odd expressions on faces, but Wood wanted to make sure fans knew they were fake. Posting on Twitter he replied to the images writing, "this is AI BS". Following his post, the social media site has now added a label confirming the detail.

Recent findings suggest that the only official images we've had of the upcoming Lord of the Rings movie come from a behind-the-scenes video posted by Warner Bros. Shared in September, these feature fresh looks at the Shire as well as a glimpse at the back of Frodo's head.

In a recent development, andy Serkis recently shared another glimpse at the set to mark the end of filming. While this didn't contain any footage from the movie, it did feature the actors' Gollum voice once again.

The Lord of the Rings: The Hunt for Gollum hits theaters December 17, 2027, the same day as Avengers: Secret Wars. For more, check out our guide to how to watch the Lord of the Rings movies in order.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Nioh 3 is one of the most anticipated games of 2026, and it’s easily among the biggest releases of February. We’re a few days away from the start of that month, however, but we don’t have to wait until then to actually play Team Ninja’s next major release.

The previously confirmed demo has arrived, and it’s one any fan of action games should check out, especially if you missed the PlayStation-exclusive beta held last year.

Sources indicate that unlike previous tests, the Nioh 3 demo is available on PC and PS5, just like the main game. This is pretty new for the series, which has typically launched first on PlayStation before coming to PC months later.

Recent findings suggest that the Nioh 3 demo includes a decent portion of content from the beginning of the game. It’s enough to show off the core duality mechanic, letting you switch between the Samurai and Ninja styles at will. It also includes a preview of the game’s open field level design, which makes it sit somewhere between full open world and the more linear level design of past Nioh games.

Feedback from the previous beta has been implemented into the demo (and full release), so you may see some familiar faces, as well as areas you visited before - assuming you played that one.

Another big reason why you might want to grab the Nioh 3 demo is that your progress in it will carry over to the full version. This includes the character creator, too, meaning you can spend all day perfecting your character without having to worry about missing out on playing the actual game.

It has been revealed that the demo even supports online multiplayer for up to three players, in case you come to Nioh for co-op. If you complete the available content, you’ll earn an in-game bonus in the full version. This is something Team Ninja has done with past Nioh titles, of course.

This time, your reward is the Twin-Snake Helmet. Just make sure you complete the demo before February 15.

Nioh 3 is out February 6 on PC, and PlayStation 5.

Stanford scientists discover 3 hidden brain types behind ADHD and anxiety

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1193 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A new Stanford Medicine-led study has identified three distinct biological brain types, known as biotypes, in children with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), anxiety disorder or both conditions.
  • The findings could help unravel the complicated relationship between two of the most common childhood mental health disorders, which frequently share symptoms.
  • In a recent development, by examining thousands of functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) scans, researchers identified three biological patterns associated with different groups of symptoms.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A new Stanford Medicine-led study has identified three distinct biological brain types, known as biotypes, in children with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), anxiety disorder or both conditions.

The findings could help unravel the complicated relationship between two of the most common childhood mental health disorders, which frequently share symptoms. Published recently in Nature Mental Health, the study reveals that each biotype involves disruptions in a different set of brain circuits.

In a recent development, by examining thousands of functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) scans, researchers identified three biological patterns associated with different groups of symptoms. These findings could eventually help doctors recognize ADHD and anxiety earlier, identify latest targets for treatment, and determine which therapies are most likely to benefit individual patients.

"The high overlap between ADHD and anxiety actually hinders our understanding of the neurobiology underlying traditional, symptom-based diagnoses," noted co-senior study author Yu Zhang, PhD, assistant professor of psychiatry and behavioral sciences.

Doctors right now rely on symptom checklists to diagnose ADHD and anxiety. However, Zhang explained that children diagnosed with either disorder frequently experience symptoms associated with the other.

Looking Beyond Traditional ADHD and Anxiety Diagnoses.

It has been revealed that yong Jiao, PhD, a postdoctoral scholar at the University of Iowa, is the study's lead author. Zhang shares senior authorship with Jing Jiang, PhD, assistant professor of pediatric neurology at the University of Iowa.

"We wanted to know whether the biological differences among children with ADHD and anxiety follow the diagnostic labels used in the clinic," Zhang said.

According to recent reports, the researchers found that the relationship was not so straightforward. Children diagnosed with ADHD, anxiety or both could belong to any of the three brain biotypes, although some biological patterns were more prevalent among children with particular diagnoses.

According to the researchers, identifying these underlying differences could add a valuable layer of biological information to existing diagnostic categories, benefiting both future research and clinical care.

AI Uncovers Hidden Patterns in Thousands of Brain Scans.

Industry observers note that the research team drew on data from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development study, an ongoing investigation of brain development involving more than 11,000 children across the United States. Participants were 9 or 10 years old when they entered the project.

In a recent development, the analysis included 3,508 children who already had a diagnosis of ADHD, anxiety or both when they enrolled, along with 693 children who initially had neither diagnosis but subsequently developed one or both conditions. Another 1,947 children who never received either diagnosis served as a control group.

It has been revealed that all participants underwent fMRI brain scans and completed a series of cognitive and behavioral assessments. To independently validate their findings, the scientists examined brain scans from another 224 children participating in a separate research project called the Healthy Brain Network. Each child in this additional group had been diagnosed with ADHD or anxiety disorder.

The team developed an artificial intelligence model to investigate functional connectivity, which describes how different regions of the brain work together. By incorporating diagnostic information and behavioral test results, the model identified patterns of brain connectivity that were more pronounced in children with ADHD, anxiety or both compared with those who had neither condition.

Combining behavioral information with brain imaging data revealed two major dimensions of dysfunction associated with ADHD and anxiety: cognitive-behavioral dysfunction and emotion-attention dysfunction.

Each dimension involves a different network of brain regions. Different combinations of these disruptions produced three distinct biotypes, which the researchers named the externalizing-disinhibited biotype, the internalizing-distressed biotype and the mixed biotype.

Three Distinct Brain Types and Their Symptoms.

The three biological categories were mutually exclusive (each child was in only one biotype), but none was limited to a particular traditional diagnosis.

Recent findings suggest that children belonging to the externalizing-disinhibited group tended to exhibit higher levels of impulsivity, hostility, defiance, aggression and rule-breaking behavior. ADHD diagnoses were more common among children in this group.

The internalizing-distressed group was characterized by greater feelings of guilt and tension, stronger perfectionist tendencies, and more symptoms associated with anxiety and depression. Children with this biological profile were more frequently diagnosed with anxiety disorders.

According to recent reports, those in the mixed group experienced more difficulties with attention, irritability and self-injury. Like children in the externalizing-disinhibited group, they were more likely to have an ADHD diagnosis.

Despite these tendencies, researchers found every combination of brain biotype and conventional diagnosis among the children they studied.

Brain Changes Could Reveal ADHD and Anxiety Before Diagnosis.

One of the most surprising findings emerged when scientists examined brain scans taken from children who had not been diagnosed with ADHD or anxiety when they first entered the study.

The distinctive biological patterns were already detectable in their initial scans, even though the children did not receive a diagnosis of ADHD, anxiety or both until later.

"We think this means we may be able to use the biotypes as an early indicator of these conditions," Zhang said, noting that identifying these patterns before diagnosis was the most unexpected aspect of the research. "It could help us provide more timely intervention for these conditions and slow down or, we hope, even reverse their progression.".

Toward More Personalized ADHD and Anxiety Treatments.

Zhang does not expect the newly identified brain biotypes to replace conventional diagnoses based on symptoms. Instead, combining the two approaches could help clinicians select treatments that are better suited to individual children.

Sources indicate that finding an effective treatment for ADHD or anxiety currently involves considerable experimentation. Children may need to try several medications before discovering which one provides meaningful relief.

Recent findings suggest that "When doctors prescribe a new medication, it can take quite a long time -- a couple of weeks or months -- to see a response," Zhang said. "If the first medication doesn't work, they switch to a different one".

This process can be lengthy, expensive and frustrating.

Industry observers note that zhang hopes future clinical trials will build on the team's findings by investigating how different treatments affect specific patterns of brain activity. Such studies could eventually help researchers determine which therapies are most effective for each of the three biotypes.

"We want to find biomarkers that can really inform the right treatment at the right time," he mentioned.

Researchers involved in the study are affiliated with Stanford University's Wu Tsai Neurosciences Institute and the Stanford Institute for Human-Centered AI.

Additional contributors came from the University of Iowa, the University of Texas at Austin and the University of Pennsylvania Perelman School of Medicine.

The research received funding from the National Institutes of Health (grant numbers R01MH129694, R01MH136197, R01MH145082, R01MH140425, U24AA021697, R01DA057567, R37MH101495 and R01MH132784), the Eagles Autism Foundation, the Stanford Knight Initiative for Brain Resilience, the Rosenkranz Foundation, the Brain and Behavior Research Foundation, and the Effie and Wofford Cain Foundation.

Materials provided by Stanford Medicine. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Fnatic has confirmed the departure of its longest-serving player, jungler Razork, who is set to join Team Heretics. With support Lospa also set to leave, the London club faces a near-total LEC roster rebuild for 2027.

Recent findings suggest that fnatic has made its first confirmed exit official as it rebuilds its LEC roster for 2027. Razork was the London club’s longest-serving player and its main playmaker. He leaves after five seasons in the jungle.

Industry observers note that the club marked the departure with a farewell video titled “Thank You, Iván”. In it, Fnatic recalls him arriving as a young player with huge ambition. He had entered the LEC with Misfits Gaming in 2020 before moving to Fnatic in 2022. The club later extended his contract to run through 2026.

Sources indicate that his next stop appears to be Team Heretics. Sheep Esports reported that the 26-year-old will play alongside midlaner Jackies and support Jun. Heretics had already tried to sign him a year earlier. On that occasion it agreed a buyout with Fnatic but could not agree terms with the player.

The rebuild runs deeper than the jungle. Every Fnatic team member except Lospa was due out of contract in 2026. The support was signed until the end of 2027.

In a recent development, that deal will not keep him at Fnatic either. Lospa has reportedly agreed verbally to join SK Gaming for 2027. No buyout is involved in moving his contract between the two clubs. With that move, the one contract running beyond 2026 also leaves the club.

In the jungle, Yike is set to replace Razork in a 2027 line-up of Soboro, Yike, Vladi, Doggo and Labrov, according to Sheep Esports sources.

Recent findings suggest that the overhaul follows a difficult year. Fnatic finished eighth in LEC 2026 Versus. It then placed seventh in Spring, which ended on 10 May. Summer brought the same finishing position.

A loss to GIANTX on 30 August kept the team out of the Summer playoffs. That defeat left the club absent from Worlds for the first time since 2016.

According to recent reports, 5 years of memories. it was an honour to see you grow into the person and player you are 🧡 https://t.co/F3TWY9WZqq pic.twitter.com/K3K3EQICZ1.

— FNATIC (@FNATIC) November 17, 2026.

For the UK scene, the scale of change matters. Fnatic is one of the LEC’s best-supported clubs among British fans.

The club has also opened a search for a League of Legends General Manager. Its job advert states Fnatic goes into a rebuild in 2027. The new hire will run recruitment of players, coaches and staff, including transfers and benchings, and will manage the team’s budget.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A judge has denied a motion to dismiss a US lawsuit against chip makers Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron.
  • Recent findings suggest that the class action suit was filed at the United States District Court for the Northern District of California in June this year.
  • It has been revealed that the trio of companies deny having colluded, arguing in a latest motion to have the case dismissed (thanks, IGN) that this suit simply retreads old ground covered in a previous antitrust case and quoting deceased judge Richard Posner.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A judge has denied a motion to dismiss a US lawsuit against chip makers Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron. The suit acccuses the companies of fixing RAM prices and supply, thereby contributing to worsening the effects of the ongoing memory crisis.

Recent findings suggest that the class action suit was filed at the United States District Court for the Northern District of California in June this year. It accuses Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron of moving in lockstep away from production of consumer-focused DDR3 and DDR4 RAM and towards HBM memory more typically used in AI datacenters. The suit claims that "in a competitive commodity market", "at least one of three large producers, seeing record prices, would expand output of the product whose price was rising", thereby forcing their competitors to either follow suit or risk losing out on customers.

It has been revealed that the trio of companies deny having colluded, arguing in a latest motion to have the case dismissed (thanks, IGN) that this suit simply retreads old ground covered in a previous antitrust case and quoting deceased judge Richard Posner. "[C]ompetitors in concentrated markets watch each other like hawks," was the Posner quote they wheeled out, which I mention because otherwise the response I'm about to lay out will sound like a very weird tangent.

Recent findings suggest that "But Plaintiffs’ allegations go beyond hawks watching each other," judge Noël Wise wrote in her order to deny the dismissal motion. "Their contentions are more akin to hawks flying in formation – an activity that hawks ordinarily do not do.".

You know a case is getting serious when facts about Avian behaviour start being wheeled out in response to similes. Bird chatter aside, all this decision means is that the case will rumble on, with both sides still having a chance to present more evidence or make points in their favour before any eventual decision is made by the courts.

So, shelve any hopes you might have of a rapid solution to the memory crisis, which at the moment looks likely to last until at least 2028.

#155357. 10 Elements Metroidvanias Could Borrow From GTA 6

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1615 w)

10 Elements Metroidvanias Could Borrow From GTA 6

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1615 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dualshockers

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As someone who usually writes about Metroidvanias but has recently been engrossed in GTA 6, I haven't stopped thinking about the points where the two converge.
  • Rockstar's upcoming work isn't an adventure like the series' previous iterations; instead, it boasts an even finer and more meticulous design that, at fleeting moments, makes me feel it hides lessons beyond the obvious.
  • That games in its genre will follow in its footsteps is logical, but I truly believe there's a sufficiently diverse level of excellence to consider that not only open-world titles will benefit from its influence.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As someone who usually writes about Metroidvanias but has recently been engrossed in GTA 6, I haven't stopped thinking about the points where the two converge.

Rockstar's upcoming work isn't an adventure like the series' previous iterations; instead, it boasts an even finer and more meticulous design that, at fleeting moments, makes me feel it hides lessons beyond the obvious.

That games in its genre will follow in its footsteps is logical, but I truly believe there's a sufficiently diverse level of excellence to consider that not only open-world titles will benefit from its influence.

Therefore, in order to return to writing about the type of games I'm passionate about while still fulfilling my communicative responsibility towards the interactive entertainment industry's latest titan, here are ten elements Metroidvanias could borrow from GTA 6.

Throughout its history, Grand Theft Auto has been a franchise of journeys, stories, and mechanics that unfold along the way rather than at the destination, giving vehicles a prominent role as in GTA 6.

In contrast, movement in Metroidvanias, despite the notable importance of exploration, is reduced to the characters and their abilities, limiting the worlds' scale to the equally slow speed at which their protagonists move.

Therefore, as the final stages of each campaign approach, fast travel becomes the key to backtracking, so the presence of manually controllable means of transport would not only add another layer of depth but also enable even larger worlds.

It doesn't have to be permanent, of course, as I personally love concrete maps that you can traverse on foot, yet the genre would benefit from a broader understanding of distance than it has been done so far.

Although I don't believe every game should have a plethora of minigames and side activities like GTA 6, I do think they highlight the narrow imagination with which Metroidvanias approach their gameplay concepts.

Speaking of verbs, fighting and moving are the only ones that can be attributed to their vast majority, instead of including more interactive elements that would help diversify the gaming experience.

Silver Pines, for example, does an excellent job in this regard by inheriting puzzles from horror games, but visual novels' decision-making, RPGs' morality systems, or stealth games' infiltrative sections could have a place in the right products.

Of course, it's easier to have diverse gameplay if you're an open-world game than if you're an action-adventure title, since the classification limits you, though I think it's a good time to break free from the shackles of labels.

Especially since FromSoftware's games have influenced the genre, it's become increasingly difficult to find a Metroidvania with a concrete story, told linearly and directly rather than through contextual and ambiguous elements.

These are rich and fertile narrative mechanisms for creating immersive worlds, no doubt, but the trope easily becomes exhausted after practically everyone resorts to it to tell their tales.

I'm not necessarily talking about cinematics or actors with impressive performances, but about campaigns with concrete beginnings, developments, and endings, as Prince of Persia: The Lost Crown and Ori and the Blind Forest have already done.

These examples demonstrate that it's achievable, and if we dare to go further and adopt a love story as emotional and sensitive as Jason and Lucia's, all the better.

Returning to the premise of gameplay variety, Metroidvanias have failed to convey the influence of their environments beyond the visual, as our ways of interacting with different biomes remain virtually unchanged.

You don't usually dive into aquatic biomes, just as you don't climb mountainous areas or sink into swamps, because the way we orient ourselves in space tends to be the same regardless of that location's unique characteristics.

In contrast, GTA 6 does a superb job of differentiating each of its regions, with activities adapted to the physical attributes of each one to truly convey the feeling that the world you're inhabiting exists.

I'm not suggesting the same level of depth or technological detail, but rather the same approach: to turn aesthetic beauty into playable immersion.

GTA 6, with its massive wardrobe and extensive customization system, reminded me of how special it felt to see Alucard's simple cape color change in Castlevania: Symphony of the Night depending on his equipment.

When you think of the greatest Metroidvanias, we all know and play the same protagonist, from their visual presentation to their gameplay styles, as the options are kept to a minimum to ensure precision and refinement.

It's a perfectly valid design sacrifice, and it has given us countless masterpieces, yet invalidating player expression by not allowing them to create their own unique gameplay and aesthetic combinations is a debt that has gone unpaid for years.

It's easier mentioned than done, considering how much more difficult it is to conceive of an avatar that offers so many alternatives, but it's so captivating in GTA 6 that I can't help but dream with the possibility.

Even with the perpetual satire and exaggeration inherent in GTA 6's story, it reminded me how unusual realistic narratives have become within the video game industry, which is at the mercy of various forms of fantasy instead.

Thus, would playing a Metroidvania governed by our universal laws be even remotely as entertaining as one with an entirely new world? I don't have the slightest idea, precisely because this approach is so unexplored within the genre.

The conversations between Jason and Lucia feel so human, as do many of the events with NPCs and secondary characters, that you empathize almost instinctively, leading to a level of connection unusual in Metroidvanias.

Works like Shadow Complex or, to a lesser extent, Silver Pines itself, partially demonstrate this possibility, and I feel that exploring it would help open up a completely unique avenue for the genre, one that isn't limited to hand-drawn 2D side-scrollers.

Sources indicate that among the most striking aspects of GTA 6 is the way every NPC reacts to your every move. Whether it's walking, wearing unusual clothing, drawing a weapon, or saying something, there's an interaction waiting for you around every corner.

In the context of Metroidvanias, games like Hollow Knight have already explored the idea of characters responding to our actions, and even with the system's restrictions, it's an integral element of its worldbuilding.

Accordingly, building on that foundation and with an eye on Leonida's organic world, campaigns can be created where we feel our influence isn't rigidly predetermined but rather gradually constructed on both a macro and micro level.

It's difficult to anticipate the rapid arrival of a structure with such ramifications due to the predominance of independent developers in the genre, though simply having the horizon in sight is enough to begin moving towards it.

Ever since I played The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim, I've realized that progression in video games is almost always extradiegetic—that is, it happens before the player's eyes, not so much the character's—and GTA 6 also rejected this principle.

Consequently, "finding" a skill instead of developing it is a statement in itself about how a character grows, which is quite functional for the Metroidvania philosophy but not so much for the feeling of evolving through our gameplay experience.

I doubt it's interesting to lock the double jump behind having to go to the gym and do jumping jacks for a whole week, yet a game where our combat and movement skills expand based on how we interact with its base mechanics is a future that excites me.

GTA 6 makes it very simple, and sometimes it's even annoying, but the fact that it works here for the sake of realism doesn't mean that Metroidvanias can't use the same methodology for the sake of fun.

In Metroidvanias, there's no such thing as approaches: you either play the way the game wants you to, or you simply have to give up on the possibility of finishing it altogether.

GTA 6, inevitably, is also a slave to determinism, yet it leans slightly towards immersive sim design, allowing you to choose how you're going to fulfill your unchangeable obligations.

There are fights you can avoid with dialogue, wars you can replace with stealthy takedowns, and conflicts you can relocate with distraction tactics, thanks in part to a level design that offers more than one way to handle its execution.

I would never ask a Metroidvania to be Dishonored, though I could respectfully request that it at least try to integrate the possibility that not every challenge is solved by depleting a boss's health bar or completing an artificial platforming challenge.

I'd be lying if I didn't say I'm quite a fan of the true ending trope hidden behind an obscure side mission that unfolds outside the main campaign, but it does sadden me that it's the only option Metroidvanias often display.

While GTA 6 emphasizes numerous decisions, circumstances, and systems that occur at pivotal points in the plot and throughout the game, Metroidvanias have a much more reductive model.

Regardless of how you play, games in this genre tend to follow the formula of "good ending, bad ending by changing a decision before the final boss, true ending behind an optional mission", and it's starting to lose its appeal.

Certainly, GTA 6's approach isn't necessarily revolutionary or life-changing, yet it's complex enough to make you think about how you interact with its systems, so it more than achieves its goal.

Sources indicate that of course, for there to be impactful decisions to make, it's necessary to apply several of the fundamentals mentioned in this list, as they can't be achieved in isolation. However, since Rockstar's game will surely be the benchmark for many years to come, I'm sure some lessons will sink in.

There are more than 160 different abilities to experiment with across this quirky roguelite, so the only limit is your imagination!

Download now! Everything is Crab.

Thankfully, you've got your trusty crocodile bestie named Yeti to help you on your journey, along with a variety of guns and abilities to level up. And if all that action hasn't gotten your interest piqued yet, then the talking crocodile most definitely will.

#155354. Latest Update: Too much of this common nutrient could be accelerating blood vessel aging

Latest Update: Too much of this common nutrient could be accelerating blood vessel aging

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (997 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that blood vessels naturally become less flexible with age, and certain diseases can accelerate this process.
  • Sources indicate that one factor that can contribute to this damage is an excess of phosphate in the bloodstream.
  • In a recent development, scientists at the University of Colorado Anschutz School of Medicine have identified a kidney protein that plays a critical role in regulating blood phosphate levels.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that blood vessels naturally become less flexible with age, and certain diseases can accelerate this process. As blood vessels stiffen, the risk of cardiovascular disease and premature death increases.

Sources indicate that one factor that can contribute to this damage is an excess of phosphate in the bloodstream. Although elevated blood phosphate (hyperphosphatemia) is relatively uncommon in the general population, it occurs much more frequently in people with chronic kidney disease (CKD), whose kidneys gradually lose their ability to filter waste from the blood.

In a recent development, scientists at the University of Colorado Anschutz School of Medicine have identified a kidney protein that plays a critical role in regulating blood phosphate levels. The discovery could have particularly important implications for people living with CKD.

In a fresh study published in October 2026, the researchers found that a deficiency of this protein caused blood vessels to stiffen more rapidly and shortened lifespan in animal models. These effects were especially pronounced when the animals consumed a diet high in phosphate. Reducing phosphate intake helped alleviate some of the damage.

Sources indicate that the findings point to a potential upcoming target for medications and other therapies designed to maintain healthy phosphate levels. Such treatments could eventually help people with CKD improve their overall health and potentially live longer.

Industry observers note that "Phosphate is really underestimated in terms of longevity in all mammals. The higher the concentration of phosphate in the blood, the shorter the lifespan," says Makoto Miyazaki, PhD, a research professor in the Division of Renal Diseases and Hypertension and the senior author of the new study.

How Excess Phosphate Accelerates Blood Vessel Aging.

Industry observers note that phosphorus is an essential nutrient that helps build and maintain strong bones. It occurs naturally in a wide variety of whole foods, including meat, poultry, fish, whole grains, nuts, legumes, and dairy products, generally in the form of organic phosphate compounds. Food manufacturers also add phosphates to processed foods and beverages to improve flavor and extend shelf life.

Although phosphorus is necessary for good health, excessive levels in the blood (hyperphosphatemia) can trigger a series of damaging biological changes. Phosphate additives may be particularly concerning because the body absorbs them more rapidly and efficiently than the organic phosphates naturally present in whole foods.

In a recent development, persistently elevated phosphate levels can cause smooth muscle cells within blood vessel walls to behave more like cells responsible for building bone. As a result, these cells begin depositing calcium phosphate crystals resembling those found in bones, causing the blood vessels to harden (or calcify).

Healthy blood vessels are flexible, allowing them to expand and contract in response to changing blood flow demands. Calcification compromises this flexibility, effectively accelerating vascular aging and potentially contributing to numerous age-related health problems throughout the body.

A Hidden Protein Helps Maintain Phosphate Balance.

Industry observers note that under normal circumstances, the kidneys remove excess phosphate from the bloodstream before it reaches harmful levels. As CKD progresses, however, declining kidney function makes it increasingly difficult for the body to eliminate phosphate and other substances.

It has been revealed that maintaining the right amount of phosphate requires continuous adjustments. After the kidneys filter phosphate from the blood, a portion is eliminated through urine, while the remainder is returned to the circulation. A protein known as NPT2A is responsible for reabsorbing approximately 75% of the filtered phosphate, preventing the body from losing too much phosphorus.

When phosphate levels are already elevated, however, this recycling mechanism can become problematic. Miyazaki and his colleagues discovered that another protein, called TMEM174, acts as a natural brake on this process. By binding to NPT2A, it limits the amount of phosphate being reabsorbed into the bloodstream.

Protein Deficiency Shortens Lifespan in Animal Models.

In a recent development, the latest findings highlight the importance of TMEM174 in maintaining healthy phosphate levels. Animals deficient in the protein struggled to regulate phosphate in their blood, experienced increased vascular calcification, and had significantly shorter lifespans.

It has been revealed that "We don't fully understand how yet, but somehow TMEM174 is destabilizing NPT2A," says Miyazaki. "And without enough TMEM174, homeostasis is disrupted.".

A deficiency of TMEM174 appears to result primarily from genetic factors rather than chronic kidney disease itself. However, the research suggests that people with CKD who also have insufficient levels of this protein could be particularly vulnerable to the harmful effects of excess phosphate.

A Potential Fresh Target for Protecting Blood Vessels.

Miyazaki hopes the discovery will lead to treatments that reduce the amount of excess phosphate the kidneys return to the bloodstream.

Dietary changes may provide some benefit, particularly by reducing consumption of fast food, deli meats, sodas, and other processed products that contain large amounts of phosphate. However, Miyazaki explains that managing phosphate levels through diet alone can be challenging, especially for people with CKD. Because phosphate is present in such a wide range of foods, avoiding it is virtually impossible.

In future research, Miyazaki plans to investigate these kidney proteins further, along with the hormones involved in maintaining the body's chemical balance. He also wants to better understand why calcium accumulation in blood vessels is so common among people with CKD.

Recent findings suggest that for now, identifying the role of TMEM174 represents an important advance in understanding how the body regulates phosphate. It could also help lay the groundwork for upcoming approaches to improving the health of people whose phosphate balance is disrupted.

"Scientists have been studying phosphate homeostasis for over 100 years, so to still find a new protein that regulates phosphate is kind of unique," says Miyazaki.

In a recent development, missions that permanently boost max Health, Stamina, and Focus in GTA 6 appear in a few places. However, you'll never know there's a buff until you complete them and all but one are hidden away, meaning you'll need to find them by chance or get lucky.

Industry observers note that as well as being worth seeking them out if you want to buff your stats, they also include some of the best and weirdest missions in the game, so it's a double win if you do go after them. I've not included the meditation spots in GTA 6 that also boost your max Focus here, as that's a whole thing in its own right.

It has been revealed that the map above highlights where you you start each mission. Some are single hit jobs where you do one thing and get the boost, others require a few steps and you might have to wait to continue.

Sources indicate that I've covered the whole GTA 6 aliens thing fully already, but the short version is you need to be abducted (the map indicates where it happened for me), by looking out for an abandoned car at night with all its light flashing. After that you need to sleep, where a dream will show you the rest of the way. Read my full guide for all the details but completing this will permanently increase your Health, Stamina, and Focus.

The GTA 6 Final Flush mission can be started by scanning the QR code you find in the bathroom marked above. It's at Corsair Key, near where you start the game. Once you've done that you'll get a second marker to meet someone at a waffle house. Read our guide for the full walkthrough, but at the end of it you'll come out with a permanent increase in max Stamina.

This is the only mission that's pointed out to you when you scan the crop dusting poster outside the motel reception in chapter 2. This will direct you to McKittrick Farm marked on the map above. You'll need to dust the crops first but that will then lead to a mission later where you need to get some chemicals. Complete that and you'll have the chance to eat a mutated strawberry that will permanently increase your max Stamina. You'll get a text later to close out this mission and, while there are no more stat boosts, I highly recommend seeing how it all ends.

According to recent reports, the Circles of Hell mission sees you visit Satan and blow him away Doom style. You'll need to find the garage marked above in Port Gellhorn somewhere around midnight. You'll know it's the right time because it'll be open and lit up red. Talk to the people inside and go with them to meet the dark lord and kill him. If you fail at all at this point, check the wooden throne for some more 'shrooms so you can try again. Defeat the hordes and you'll get a permanent increase to your max Health, plus a shotgun and t-shirt.

Weekly digests, tales from the communities you love, and more.

Recent findings suggest that if you head all the way out to Lake Tallaloko north of Milliport you'll find a logging yard full of felled trees. Make your way to the location on the map and you'll find a yellow shipping crate you can enter. At least one person here at GR reported needing the cut-off tool in GTA 6 to open it, but when I found it (before having the tool) it was just open. Inside you'll find a mysterious psychedelic box you can interact with. Do that and you'll have to complete a trippy obstacle course made of crates and logs. Get through it and you'll get a permanent max Stamina increase and new tattoo.

According to recent reports, head roughly to this area on the map (near where you can get abducted by aliens at night) and listen out for shouting and gunfire in the woods, near the road construction site. Here you’ll find a group of self-proclaimed ‘ecologists’ doing some environmental hunting of invasive species. Pick up the Duke 556 Assault Rifle on the barrel to begin the ‘practice round’ shooting static targets such as pumpkins, and then you’ll be prompted to wager $250 on the main challenge - shooting a bunch of iguanas released from a cage. Win and you'll get $250 plus a max Focus increase.

  • Industry observers note that this newly introduced mode, Free Play, not only allows for local multiplayer of up to four players (with either humans or CPUs racing together), but also for complete freedom of choice in vehicle, character and planet to race on.

In a recent development, split-screen multiplayer is often treated by developers as a forgotten vestige of a bygone age, something to be left behind as the standardisation of online play makes it redundant, especially following the pandemic. It's considered unlikely that you'll have another human being in your home to pick up a controller with you, and since you've inevitably got an internet connection, why not just use that to connect to anyone in the world? I find there's a unique beauty in playing something shoulder to shoulder on a couch with another person, and it seems Fuse Games sees that light too, with Star Wars: Galactic Racer set to be updated to add local splitscreen multiplayer sometime early next year.

Industry observers note that this newly introduced mode, Free Play, not only allows for local multiplayer of up to four players (with either humans or CPUs racing together), but also for complete freedom of choice in vehicle, character and planet to race on. A simple versus mode like this is a far cry from the roguelite structure of the main game, and one that draws it closer to its arcade racing game roots. An embracing of that is always welcome, as Galactic Racer has been a reminder to many of just how wonderful the arcade racing genre can be, and how poorly served its been in the industry for a while. For example, while the Fuse Games team is partly made up of Criterion Games veterans, Criterion itself has recently been folded into being a Battlefield Studio by EA, making the future of Need for Speed and Burnout uncertain.

As for why this feature may not have been available at launch, other than the cynical view that it wasn't considered a moneymaking priority for Fuse Games and Secret Mode, CD Projekt Red senior technical producer Shayna Moon weighed in to theorise that it took some effort to get four separately-rendered views of the game running without making their machine explode like the Death Star. As Moon puts it: "To be overly simple about it, if the game is running at 30fps for each player, that means it’s actually rendering 120fps." Likely not an matter for a lot of PC players, but a potential issue for console players considering the game is built to run at a locked 60fps for one player on consoles. Past this upcoming patch, it looks like the Star Wars franchise as a whole could be set for more smaller games ala Galactic Racer in general, per comments made by Lucasfilms' vice president.

Latest Update: Break up and re-commodify a fallen Earth in Steel Gullet, a satisfyingly funereal factory puzzler that really loves thermodynamics

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (664 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rockpapershotgun

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It's amazing what a difference a few lines of preamble can make to your understanding of a game.
  • In a recent development, the difference is that you're doing this inside a huge walking fortress city, which stamps across the surface of a largely unseen, devastated and uninhabitable Earth.
  • It has been revealed that from a certain, carefully limited point of view, this transforms Steel Gullet into the kind of "Zen experience" I hope death-positive morticians have when really absorbed in their work.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It's amazing what a difference a few lines of preamble can make to your understanding of a game. Out now on PC, Steel Gullet is a factory engineering puzzler that, while notable for its meticulous interest in thermodynamics, broadly compares to the foundational work of Zachtronics, together with more recent and focussed conveyor belt wranglers such as Modulus. Resources come in, and you arrange machines on a grid to transform them into something else, before sliding them into an output hopper.

In a recent development, the difference is that you're doing this inside a huge walking fortress city, which stamps across the surface of a largely unseen, devastated and uninhabitable Earth. Your resources are the refuse of a bygone human civilisation: knots of concrete and rebar, flaccid rubber hose and splintered plank, that must be separated out before you can manufacture anything.

It has been revealed that from a certain, carefully limited point of view, this transforms Steel Gullet into the kind of "Zen experience" I hope death-positive morticians have when really absorbed in their work. My task is to lay a civilisation to rest, by dissecting and cleansing the remains, readying a fallen objectworld for an after-life that extends somewhere beyond the map's huge rusty walls (walls that, perhaps appropriately, constrain your camera movement a bit too much for comfort).

Industry observers note that it makes me think of the vertigo I get when I look at devices such as, well, the computer I'm writing this on, and think about how many materials and histories of production lie entangled within it. Steel Gullet answers the desire for clarity and accounting there. Of course, the other part of the premise is that I am doing busywork for some kind of totalitarian organisation, G.R.I.D. But shh, no time to think about that! I'm trying to work out how hot rubber needs to be before it can be moulded.

Thermodynamics is Steel Gullet's fixation, and a worthwhile one. Every material encased in each lump of salvage has different physical properties – a melting point, density, solubility, ferromagnetism, etcetera. You meed to exploit these differences to separate the pieces. Wood, for example, is more buoyant than metal and concrete, so if you feed the clump into an oil bath, the planks will float to the top. If there's rubber, you can run the clump through furnaces to melt and drain it, then cool and reheat the resulting puddle to create a malleable material.

It's still just the usual automation game routine of funnelling greebly wotsits through various smashy boxes to produce a commodity. But the thermodynamics sim element both supports the above feeling of purifying a hopelessly muddled world, and makes for a surprising visual feast: I enjoy watching each material emerge from the inital jumble and assume different shapes. There are the usual supporting infrastructure elements, such as elevators, splitters and manual junction boxes. I dare say somebody will build a logic circuit in Steel Gullet, sooner or later - let's start the clock till they get Doom running on the thing.

In terms of overall strategy, you alternate between sending outputs to hoppers that earn you cash, and sending them to hoppers that generate research progression. You'll also unlock new rooms, removing walls and exposing new output hoppers. As you're issued new work orders, you must break open your production lines to install new machines and redirect the flow. Fortunately, you can sell back components to keep your cash reserves healthy – or at least, you can in the demo.

In a recent development, between chapters, you'll be invited to join the resistance against the aforesaid G.R.I.D., perhaps sending information to the rebels. But again, no time, no time! I have all this concrete I need to powderise, all these girders I need to liquefy and make fresh, all these crisp, gleaming circuitboards I need to manufacture. The city's hunger is as vast as it is holy. Read more on Steam.

GTA 6 Workers Union Survived Execs, But Drowned at the Shore

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Rockstar Games has had an incredible week following the launch of GTA 6, but the same can't be said for the developers who were hoping to secure formal recognition for their union.
  • As VGC reports, the ballot had a high turnout among the roughly 1,600 eligible employees.
  • The ballot opened on November 12 and closed today, November 26.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Rockstar Games has had an incredible week following the launch of GTA 6, but the same can't be said for the developers who were hoping to secure formal recognition for their union. The results of a ballot among Rockstar's UK employees are out, and roughly three-quarters of those who voted have rejected the proposed agreement with the Independent Workers' Union of Great Britain (IWGB).

As VGC reports, the ballot had a high turnout among the roughly 1,600 eligible employees. Only 25% of votes were in favor of the deal. It's a disappointing outcome for the organizers, especially considering that they managed to get as far as negotiating an agreement with Rockstar after last year's controversial dismissals.

The ballot opened on November 12 and closed today, November 26. Had the vote gone the other way, Rockstar would have been home to the largest formally recognized union in the UK video game industry, according to the IWGB.

The negotiations weren't just about securing better salaries for GTA 6 developers. The proposed arrangement would have given staff a means of collectively negotiating everything from overtime compensation to pensions, as well as a say in how the company handles redundancies and the use of AI.

In a recent development, rockstar had already stated it would recognize the union if its staff wanted one. What makes today's outcome particularly striking is that the agreement didn't fall apart at the negotiating table. It was the vote among employees that ultimately put an end to it.

It was the vote among employees that ultimately put an end to it.

Industry observers note that speaking about the result, Rockstar's head of publishing, Jennifer Kolbe, remarked it demonstrated employees' preference for dealing directly with the company. The IWGB, meanwhile, acknowledged that it still needs to earn the confidence of more staff members.

According to recent reports, that doesn't mean the Rockstar Game Workers Union has ceased to exist, nor does it mean that employees have lost their right to join it. The union can still represent its members, but Rockstar won't be bound by the formal bargaining arrangement that was put to a vote.

It's worth remembering how unlikely it might have seemed a year ago that Rockstar's union organizers would even get to hold this vote. In October 2025, the manufacturer dismissed dozens of employees in an incident that subsequently led to an employment tribunal in the UK.

In a recent development, the IWGB alleged that the staff were targeted because of their involvement in union organizing. Rockstar, on the other hand, maintained that the dismissals were related to the sharing of confidential information on Discord. Today's ballot result doesn't settle that dispute, and the tribunal's outcome is still pending.

Recent findings suggest that the timing of the vote also makes for a rather odd contrast with what's been happening outside Rockstar's offices. GTA 6 accounted for more than half of active PS5 and Xbox players tracked by Circana on launch day, and the game has already brought in billions of dollars in retail sales.

In a recent development, for some developers, though, the question is what happens to their jobs now that the game they've spent years working on is finally out. Even the commercial success of a game as big as GTA 6 can't guarantee that there won't be redundancies further down the line. That was one of the challenges the union wanted to address before the launch.

The IWGB states it intends to keep organizing at Rockstar despite the vote. Hundreds of employees backed recognition, so the organizers aren't starting from scratch. Convincing the rest of their colleagues, however, is going to be a considerably bigger task than getting Rockstar to agree to hold the ballot in the first place.

Recent findings suggest that as with every major update, of course, there are themed activities and limited-time events throughout. Hotpot House is a cooking minigame where you attempt to run the eponymous restaurant, whereas Flavor Frenzy is series of platforming challenges that tasks you with gathering ingredients. Fortune Mahjong is a little more straightforward, with support for solo and multiplayer play.

#155343. Breaking: Common sleep and anxiety drugs could be harming aging brains

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1158 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Common sleep and anxiety drugs could be harming aging brains

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1158 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Adults age 65 and older who have dementia or other cognitive disorders are particularly vulnerable to the harmful effects of medications used to treat anxiety, sleep disturbances, psychosis, and other conditions affecting the central nervous system.
  • Potential consequences include more emergency room visits, longer and more frequent hospital stays, declining mental health, and an increased risk of premature death.
  • New research from the University at Buffalo (UB) offers some encouraging news, however.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Adults age 65 and older who have dementia or other cognitive disorders are particularly vulnerable to the harmful effects of medications used to treat anxiety, sleep disturbances, psychosis, and other conditions affecting the central nervous system.

Potential consequences include more emergency room visits, longer and more frequent hospital stays, declining mental health, and an increased risk of premature death.

New research from the University at Buffalo (UB) offers some encouraging news, however. Between 2011 and 2022, the proportion of older adults with cognitive disorders taking medications that could impair their cognitive function decreased significantly.

After analyzing data from 2,796 older adults with cognitive disorders who lived independently, researchers found that exposure to potentially inappropriate medications fell from 39.3% in 2011 to 29.3% in 2022.

In a recent development, "This is a population with some mental problems that relate to the central nervous system. These drugs also act on the central nervous system, so they can be too much for older adults if inappropriately used," notes Haowen Hsu, PharmD, a postdoctoral fellow in the Department of Pharmacy Practice at the School of Pharmacy and Pharmaceutical Sciences and first author of the study, published in the Journal of the American Geriatrics Society.

Reducing the Risks of Common Prescription Drugs.

Recent findings suggest that older adults who have spent years taking benzodiazepines such as Xanax for anxiety or sleep medications such as Ambien may benefit from a medically supervised reduction in dosage or gradual discontinuation. These medications can negatively affect cognitive function, balance, and coordination.

In a recent development, "A central word for patients in this age group is 'deprescribing,' which means, for example, removing inappropriate medications and decreasing the frequency or the dosage. In some cases, it means replacing the current medication with a milder alternative," Hsu says. "This is why it's so vital for health care providers to work closely with community pharmacists and homecare nurses to optimize medication safety.".

Industry observers note that to identify potentially problematic drugs, the research team consulted the American Geriatrics Society's Beers Criteria, which identifies approximately 100 medications that may pose risks to older adults. The researchers then concentrated specifically on medications that could present additional dangers for people with diagnosed cognitive disorders.

According to recent reports, using data from the Medical Expenditure Panel Survey, the team examined a sample representing approximately 29.7 million older Americans with cognitive disorders over the period from 2011 to 2022. They compared individuals prescribed at least one potentially inappropriate medication with those who had not received any of these drugs.

Medication Safety Has Improved, but Risks Remain.

Sources indicate that although the study did not examine what caused the decline in exposure to potentially harmful medications, Hsu points to growing awareness among researchers and clinicians over the past two decades. The gradual but sustained improvement may reflect broader advances in geriatric medicine and efforts to make prescription drug use safer.

Recent findings suggest that "We were happy to see the percentages of harm decline over that 11-year period," he indicates. "However, one-third of our target population is still exposed to these harmful medications, which isn't good.".

Older adults, even those without cognitive disorders, are particularly susceptible to harmful drug interactions and inappropriate prescriptions. In some cases, these complications can increase the risk of death. These dangers are a central focus of Team Alice, an ongoing interdisciplinary research initiative at the University at Buffalo dedicated to medication safety.

A Preventable Death Inspires Change.

Team Alice takes its name from Alice Brennan, who died in 2009 following a prescription for a muscle relaxant identified as potentially inappropriate under the Beers Criteria. The prescribing error went unrecognized within the health care system, and Brennan died following six weeks of preventable complications.

Her daughter, Mary Brennan-Taylor, shared her mother's experience with University at Buffalo researchers in the hope of bringing about systemic changes that would spare other patients and families from similar harm.

Hsu began the new study shortly after joining the university's pharmacy school and Team Alice, where he works in the UB Patient Safety Learning Laboratory.

"This work extends a series of national analyses our group has published on potentially inappropriate medications, quality of life, and health care use in older adults," notes David Jacobs, PharmD, PhD, associate professor of pharmacy practice and a principal investigator on Team Alice.

"It is especially notable as older adults with cognitive disorders are the least able to tolerate medications that worsen memory or thinking, yet nearly one in three are still receiving them. Most of these patients have a regular source of care so these medications can be identified and addressed with their care team.".

Improving Medication Safety for Older Adults.

Other contributors to the study included Team Alice's fellow principal investigators Ranjit Singh, MD, associate professor and interim chair of the Department of Family Medicine at UB's Jacobs School of Medicine and Biomedical Sciences, and Robert Wahler, PharmD, clinical associate professor of pharmacy practice.

Collin Clark, PharmD, clinical associate professor of pharmacy practice, and Steven Feuerstein, an information systems analyst at the Jacobs School, also contributed to the research.

The findings underscore the value of thorough medication reviews during routine outpatient appointments. The researchers also suggest incorporating clinical assessment tools such as the Drug Burden Index into acute and outpatient care. Such tools can help health care professionals assess the combined effects of medications that act on the central nervous system and potentially prevent avoidable complications.

Further research is needed to establish whether improving medication use can enhance quality of life and reduce hospital admissions and emergency room visits among older adults experiencing cognitive difficulties.

A Rapidly Aging Population Raises New Concerns.

The findings arrive at a significant moment in global demographic history. According to a recent report from the U.S. Census Bureau, adults age 65 and older now outnumber children from birth through age 5 worldwide for the first time in human history.

Sources indicate that however, greater longevity does not necessarily translate into more years of good health. The same report indicates that nearly 75% of adults age 65 and older have at least two chronic health conditions. Managing multiple illnesses often requires taking more medications, some of which may have detrimental effects on the aging body and brain.

It has been revealed that "This is an problem that has been building for decades, but the growth of the older adult population has arrived sooner than we expected," Hsu says. "This means that health care professionals need to pay closer attention than ever to medication safety, especially for older adults experiencing cognitive decline or other complex health concerns.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

James Marsden says his comic-accurate Cyclops suit in Avengers: Doomsday gives the audience “everything that they want to see" – even if the actor might not be feeling so snug after stepping out of the black leather.

“The comic-accurate suit was very exciting for me to do, but [they] still haven’t figured out the comfort thing yet,” Marsden told Entertainment Weekly of his brightly colored ensemble piece, which largely mirrors the X-Men leader's traditional wear.

“No, it was great. It was one of those pinch-me moments where you’re playing this iconic character and then coming back and giving the fans everything that they want to see.”.

Famously, the original X-Men trilogy cracked a joke at the expense of the superhero group's colorful array of costumes. When Hugh Jackman's Wolverine grumbled about the black leather in 2000's X-Men, Cyclops deadpanned if he would prefer "yellow spandex" instead.

It has been revealed that in recent years, Marvel Studios has given the X-Men its due on the costume front. Deadpool and Wolverine not only featured Logan in his traditional yellow and blue outfit, but also dealt Gambit a winning hand with his comic book-style suit.

With Disney's acquisition of Fox, Kevin Feige – who had a behind-the-scenes production role on the first X-Men – is finally able to make his cinematic universe dreams come true, with even Marsden admitting there had been "so much chatter" in the past about bringing the mutant team to the MCU.

So, costume? Check. A fully-fledged role instead of nostalgia bait? Check. A leading light in the final Avengers: Doomsday trailer, complete with iconic catchphrase? Check, check, and check. If you're a Cyclops fan, you'll be eating well this holiday season.

Sources indicate that unity's next venture, amidst rumours of it being bought out by the Saudi Arabian Public Investment Fund, is the Unity Fellowship, a grant program that offers $50k in cash to Unity-using indie devs that initiative release a game within a year - without asking for recoup, revenue share, creative control or IP ownership in exchange. I don't need to tell you that all sounds too good to be true, even with the Unity engine requirement, but in fairness, the organization has form for handing out cash. The Unity for Humanity grant, just earlier this year, spread $600K across ten different indie projects focused on societal and environmental problems.

Sources indicate that unity states that ten recipient studios will receive the Fellowship's cash grant, as well as direct partnership with Unity staff, industry connections, spots at Unity events and PR/marketing support. Even studios with an existing publisher can apply, if they think that "the Fellowship could still make a real difference for your game." It also clarifies that their policy regarding AI use is that "We don't require you to list the tools you used, but you must own or hold the rights to everything in your game, including any AI-generated content", which doesn't come as a huge surprise considering Unity's excitement around its Unity Spark game-generating AI tool.

In a recent development, the grant is also not open to "countries or regions subject to U.S. sanctions", such as Russia, Iran and Cuba, as well as Brazil, Italy and Quebec due to "local regulations." For developers not in those areas, applications for the grant are open until December 18th, with the recipients to be notified by the end of February 2027. If you're a developer who's interested, you can apply here.

Industry News: Scientists discover a surprising twist in how the body burns calories

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (527 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that unlike ordinary body fat, brown fat burns calories to generate heat, making it an attractive target for future obesity treatments.
  • Industry observers note that while white fat primarily serves as an energy reserve, brown adipose tissue uses energy to keep the body warm.
  • Exposure to cold naturally activates brown fat, prompting scientists to search for medications that could mimic this response.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that unlike ordinary body fat, brown fat burns calories to generate heat, making it an attractive target for future obesity treatments. Researchers at the University of Basel and University Hospital Basel have now investigated whether medication can switch on this energy-burning tissue in humans. Their surprising findings suggest that harnessing brown fat with drugs may be more challenging than anticipated.

Industry observers note that while white fat primarily serves as an energy reserve, brown adipose tissue uses energy to keep the body warm. People with more active brown fat also tend to be leaner and have better metabolic health.

Exposure to cold naturally activates brown fat, prompting scientists to search for medications that could mimic this response. A research team led by Professor Matthias Betz at the University of Basel and University Hospital Basel examined whether activating a specific receptor, known as the beta2 adrenergic receptor, could stimulate brown fat in humans. Their findings were published in the journal Cell Metabolism.

Drug Boosts Calorie Burning Without Clear Brown Fat Activation.

To investigate, the researchers conducted two experiments involving 11 healthy volunteers. They compared the effects of mild cold exposure with those of fenoterol, a medication that stimulates beta2 adrenergic receptors. The scientists measured how much energy the participants expended and used PET/CT scans to monitor brown fat activity.

Both interventions caused the body to burn more energy. However, the scans revealed an crucial difference. Only cold exposure produced clear evidence of brown fat activation, with the tissue absorbing considerably more glucose than it did following fenoterol administration.

"We were surprised that energy expenditure increased strongly with fenoterol even though we could not detect a comparable activation of brown fat," says Betz. "Our study shows that an increase in energy expenditure does not automatically mean that brown fat has been activated.".

In a recent development, exactly where the additional energy is being consumed remains a mystery. The researchers suspect that fenoterol may increase energy consumption in other tissues, potentially including skeletal muscle or white fat.

Implications for Future Weight Loss Drugs.

The findings also suggest that the biological mechanisms controlling brown fat in humans are more complex than previously thought. Analysis of human tissue indicates that fully activating brown fat may require the combined action of multiple receptors or biological signals rather than stimulating a single receptor.

Understanding these mechanisms could open new possibilities for treating obesity. Current weight loss medications work by reducing appetite. However, as people shed pounds, their bodies often compensate by burning fewer calories.

A treatment that simultaneously reduces appetite and increases calorie burning could help counteract this metabolic adaptation.

Sources indicate that "Ideally, we could combine a reduction in appetite with an increase in energy expenditure," says Betz. "But first we need a better understanding of how brown adipose tissue is regulated.".

Materials provided by University of Basel. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
