10 Great Games That Defined The Nintendo Wii

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1502 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dualshockers

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • 20 years ago, Nintendo released one of their most ambitious consoles of all time with the motion control-focused and internet connected Nintendo Wii.
  • Sources indicate that designed to be the most accessible console ever made for its era, the Wii became one of Nintendo’s greatest success stories.
  • However, Nintendo’s resurgence and the Wii’s global popularity wouldn’t have occurred had it not been for the wide variety of exclusive games that released on the console and went on to define the Wii as well as Nintendo’s future prospects.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

20 years ago, Nintendo released one of their most ambitious consoles of all time with the motion control-focused and internet connected Nintendo Wii.

Sources indicate that designed to be the most accessible console ever made for its era, the Wii became one of Nintendo’s greatest success stories. Its easy to understand controls created a phenomenon of people of all ages getting into console gaming for the first time, from children to senior citizens.

However, Nintendo’s resurgence and the Wii’s global popularity wouldn’t have occurred had it not been for the wide variety of exclusive games that released on the console and went on to define the Wii as well as Nintendo’s future prospects.

When people think of gaming rivalries, most people will think of the console wars between Nintendo and Sega in the 1980s and 1990s. While that conflict ended with the failure of the Sega Dreamcast, the two gaming brands’ mascots wouldn’t officially meet until 2007’s Mario & Sonic at the Olympic Games.

Made to coincide with the 2008 Summer Olympics in Beijing, Mario & Sonic at the Olympic Games was the first official crossover between the Super Mario and Sonic the Hedgehog franchises, with characters from both properties being able to compete in archery, fencing, rowing, and other Olympic events.

Mario & Sonic at the Olympic Games not only represents the growing comradery between Nintendo and other video game publishers but also how much pure, simplistic fun can be had on the Wii by being able to play as some of gaming’s greatest icons in jovial sports competitions.

One of the best series of games to debut with the Wii was Shigeru Miyamoto's “Wii Project” which was a series of typically Mii-centric games tailored to showcase the Wii’s controls and accessibility to more casual gamers. One of the best of these games being Wii Play.

A Wii launch title for European and Asian markets, Wii Play was essentially a Mario Party-like compilation of minigames designed to highlight the versatility of the Wiimote in games such as the Duck Hunt-like Shooting Range, Billiards, Fishing, Find Mii, and more.

Industry observers note that on a more personal note, my favorite of these minigames was the top-down Atari Combat-like Tanks! which has one or two players control tanks through toy block stages to destroy enemy tanks using the Wiimote’s D-pad.

Industry observers note that in 2006, Nintendo revolutionized mobile 2D side-scrolling Super Mario games with the release of New Super Mario Bros. for the Nintendo DS. To capitalize on that game’s success, Nintendo decided to create a multiplayer, console-based sequel, in the form of 2009’s New Super Mario Bros. Wii.

It has been revealed that the first new console-based 2D Mario game since 1995’s Super Mario World 2: Yoshi's Island, New Super Mario Bros. Wii was a near perfect translation of New Super Mario Bros. enhanced platforming gameplay to the Wii, with the added bonus of four-player local co-op featuring Mario, Luigi, Blue Toad, and Yellow Toad.

It has been revealed that in fact, Latest Super Mario Bros. Wii might have been too perfect of a game, as Nintendo essentially kept on remastering it for years on end until the release of Super Mario Bros. Wonder. The former game was essentially ported to the Wii U and Nintendo Switch in the form of New Super Mario Bros. U, New Super Luigi U, and New Super Mario Bros. U Deluxe.

Many newly introduced exclusive games made their debut on the Wii, but arguably the most creative and cinematic of them was Monolith Soft’s third-person action role-playing game Xenoblade Chronicles.

A spinoff of the long-running Xeno series, Xenoblade Chronicles is set in a sci-fi fantasy world where life eventually evolved on two titanic robots, the Bionis and the Mechonis, that have laid dormant for millennia. The situation led to lifeforms from both robots fighting each other in perpetual wars.

While Xenoblade Chronicles may not have been the best looking RPG on the market in 2010, it more than made up for its blurry visuals with its enthralling narrative, centered around the orphaned hero Shulk and his mysterious Monado sword, as well as its more open-world structured gameplay.

Ever since Nintendo released the hit fighting game Super Smash Bros. Melee on the GameCube, expectations were high for its sequel. While many players would consider Super Smash Bros. Brawl to be a disappointing sequel, it still managed to delight series newcomers in many ways.

Like previous Super Smash Bros. titles, Super Smash Bros. Brawl is a crossover fighting game pitting Nintendo’s most famous characters against each other. Brawl innovated upon the series in many ways, such as featuring non-Nintendo characters like Sonic and Snake as well as featuring a stage builder.

Industry observers note that however, what really made Brawl an epic game in the eyes of many Wii fans was its cinematic campaign, The Subspace Emissary. It depicts many of gaming's most celebrated icons fighting and joining forces together to defeat the united destructive forces of Bowser, Ganondorf, Master Hand, and Tabuu.

In a recent development, it's rare for video game series to never have a bad entry, especially one as long as Mario Kart, but the hit racing series has consistently managed to release banger after banger. In 2008, the Mario Kart game everybody needed to have was Mario Kart Wii.

The follow-up to the hit Mario Kart DS, Mario Kart Wii was innovative for the series in many ways, as it featured 24 player characters including customized Miis, motorcycles, and was the first home console MK game to feature online multiplayer.

It has been revealed that what made Mario Kart Wii especially fun and the second best-selling Wii game was its Wii Wheel accessory. While it didn’t alter gameplay in any way, the Wii Wheel helped immerse players into the feeling of actually racing with friends online and in-person.

It has been revealed that in the same vein as Wii Play, Shigeru Miyamoto strove to expand upon his “Wii Project” in 2007 by creating a game that would encourage families to exercise. He more or less succeeded with Wii Fit.

Primarily played through the packed-in Wii Balance Board, Wii Fit is a fairly relaxing exercise video game centered around players practicing yoga poses, strength training, aerobics, and balance on the Board, with the game further tracking people’s weight and fitness progress.

Wii Fit certainly didn’t make anyone exceptionally strong, but it did motivate millions of people to become more invested in their overall health, and it did lead many friends and family to start exercising together consistently.

Sources indicate that while Wii Fit didn’t make most players work up a sweat, Ubisoft Paris’ music rhythm game Just Dance certainly did, and laid the groundwork for the Wii’s longest running support. Just Dance titles would release for the console well into the eighth and ninth console generations.

Initially a Wii exclusive series, Just Dance was an expansion upon dance pad games like Dance Dance Revolution, instead having players mirror the moves of on-screen dancers as best as possible with the Wiimote tracking players' motions.

While Just Dance 1 only had a modest tracklist of 33 songs that could be played across four similar modes, it laid the groundwork for a dancing video game phenomenon that’s still going strong today; one of Ubisoft and Nintendo’s most popular series among casual and hardcore gamers alike.

Sources indicate that at Space World 2000, Nintendo publicly revealed the Super Mario 128 project as a GameCube tech demo, featuring 128 Marios running around a spherical surface. While much of this project would be utilized in Pikmin, it wasn’t fully realized until the release of 2007’s Super Mario Galaxy.

The third 3D Super Mario game, Super Mario Galaxy was one of the most ambitious entries in the franchise, as not only did it feature a more cinematic storyline centered around Rosalina and the star-like Lumas, but had players travel across the galaxy on spherical planetoids.

It has been revealed that this game design may have been nauseating for some players, but Super Mario Galaxy continued to show how the 3D Mario titles always strive to innovate upon each other to deliver creative, generation-defining experiences. The game even went on to directly inspire The Super Mario Galaxy Movie.

Without a doubt, the game that best defined the fun to be had on the Wii was arguably the greatest launch title of all time, Wii Sports.

The first entry in Shigeru Miyamoto's “Wii Project”, Wii Sports was a rather simplistic collection of sports games centered around customizable Miis playing tennis, baseball, bowling, golf, and boxing, in single-player or up to four-player local co-op.

However, Wii Sports’ simplistic design worked to its favor, as it allowed gamers of all ages and walks of life to easily play the game. The likes of Wii Sports bowling and tennis still being played by thousands of gamers worldwide 20 years later, in their original forms and within newly introduced titles in the series.

Zenless Zone Zero’s latest Special Program has delivered a tonne of information about the game’s substantial upcoming upgrade, Version 2.6. This latest addition kicks off celebrations in Newly introduced Eridu, and it’s dubbed Encore for an Old Dream.

Version 2.6 is not far off, either, arriving in ZZZ on February 6 - exactly one week from today. Encore for an Old Dream is something of an in-between story that takes place after the end of Season 2.

The narrative of 2.6 sees the Proxies’ return to Sixth Street for New Eridu's annual Gilded Carrot Day. At the centre of the celebrations is the debut of idol group Angels of Delusion at the 404 Error music venue, but not all is as it seems.

The story follows the Proxies getting invited backstage to support the group, which also includes helping them set up practice schedules, organise events and manage social media activities. There’s a rhythm minigame as part of that, along with newly introduced maps and mechanics for Marcel Adventure.

Angels of Delusion is also the group that the two upcoming Agents being introduced in this patch belong to. Members of the same group are capable of performing coordinated attacks. The new arrivals are Sunna and Aria.

Sunna is a an S-Rank Physical Support Agent who specialises in boosting teammates using Attack and Anomaly. Her Ultimate sees her pull out a giant hammer to land heavy damage, and bring teammates into combat using Quick Assist. Sunna’s companion, Bubblegum, can cast Cat's Gaze on enemies, marking them for detonation. Bubblegum can also buff the squad’s attack.

Aria is the other upcoming arrival, the group’s lead vocalist who can shift between two forms, idol projection and construct. Aria is an Ether Anomaly Agent who also deals high burst damage, specifically against enemies who suffer from any Attribute Anomalies.

Sunna and Aria also benefit from the support of the amusingly named Bangboo Biggest Fan, a fan club president who can heal them over time, and boost the squad’s Attack any time two or more Angels of Delusion members are present.

Version 2.6’s S-Rank re-runs are Yixuan (Auric Ink - Rupture), and Yuzuha (Physical - Support), who you can look forward to as part of the banners.

According to recent reports, version 2.6 will also expand Hollow Zero with a fresh game mode, Operation Matrix. The mode offers themed stages that rotate weekly, each offering new mechanics. You can now also Sweep in Hollow Zero.

Sources indicate that beyond all the celebrations, this upgrade also brings combat kit overhauls to a couple of older S-Rank characters, Lycaon and Harumasa. You can look forward to multiple limited-time events, too, including one where you can earn a new outfit for Pan Yinhu.

It has been revealed that the massive event is naturally going to be themed around Gilded Carrot Day, and it actually starts today. There’s the usual run of login rewards (about 3,300 Polychromes), as well as daily activities. Yet another login event - Gilded Surprise, Wonderful Boo-ns - will be available February 14-23, offering daily draws from a pool of 4 billion Polychrome.

As always, there’s no reason not to catch up on the latest set of Zenless Zone Zero codes for some free in-game items.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As part of a summit meeting in Manchester yesterday, the IWGB Game Workers union have joined up with other unions spanning the Republic of Ireland's GWUI, Germany's GDRT, Italy's FIOM-CGIL, France's STJV, and Spain's CSVI to publish a manifesto that aims to "bring to light the risks and dangers genAI poses to the workforce" for consumers, workers and publishers alike.

The manifesto states that "GenAI is right now harming the games industry, its workers and the games they produce," and suggests actions that can be taken by all to reduce harm done to the industry. The manifesto specifies the "severe harm to the environment, the destruction of communities and the exploitation of the Global South" as wider harms of the technology, but maintains its focus on the industry itself.

The effects of the technology on gamemakers, such as "directly and indirectly replacing workers", "worker fatigue, cognitive decline and burnout", and "a marked decline in junior positions in the industry" are listed as core harms to be avoided and fought against, with the manifesto also noting that it also "removes a sense of ownership from workers [...] the things they produce no longer feel like they have the workers' stamp on them, and therefore they can no longer take pride in them." As it states, "games are best made by people.".

Sources indicate that the manifesto goes on to explains the unions' stance that genAI is "sold to employers as an alternative to workers", and its "predisposition towards sycophancy and lack of real world context can lead to an increase in unreasonable, damaging requests when used by employers to set policy, timescales, workloads, etc., as well as to task expansion and a general degradation of conditions." In addition, its nature as a tool built on the theft of stolen third-party data is highlighted as an inherent danger, and the so-called loophole in only training models on internal data is equally highlighted as resulting in employees and creators rarely being credited or compensated for their work that is fed into the machine. This issue also ties into the inherent implicit and explicit discrimination that exists in genAI content due to datasets' "intrinsic and exclusionary Western bias that limits diversity and marginalises non-dominant languages, cultures, and ethnicities", which leads to "a homogenisation of culture.".

As for action, the manifest recommends that workers should "avoid usage of genAI services whenever possible", "distance yourself from genAI usage", and "make it clear to your employer why you do not want to use genAI", as well as, of course, to "organise. Unionise. Do it now, not when it is too late and you are already under threat." Similarly, employers are recommended to "ensure that no worker is required to use genAI", and to "disallow the use of genAI in the organization code of conduct, even for early stages of development." Finally, for consumers, it simply advises to "support games made without genAI", and to "be vocal about disliking genAI in games.".

It's an incredibly clear and concise statement that calls to mind the statement made by a selection of IGF jurors on the state of genAI in the industry and their decision not to vote for any game that uses genAI in any capacity. As both of these statements are joined in saying, "we do not have to accept the use of genAI to make video games; it is not inevitable.".

#155333. World’s largest trial of robotic knee replacement reveals surprising results

World’s largest trial of robotic knee replacement reveals surprising results

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1254 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Robotic technology can help surgeons perform knee replacement operations with greater precision, but that accuracy does not necessarily translate into better results for patients.
  • Industry observers note that robotic technology is becoming increasingly common in knee replacement surgery around the world.
  • The UK-wide RACER-Knee trial was funded by the National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR) in partnership with Stryker, the manufacturer of the robotic equipment evaluated in the study.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Robotic technology can help surgeons perform knee replacement operations with greater precision, but that accuracy does not necessarily translate into better results for patients. The RACER-Knee trial, the world's largest clinical study of its kind, found that patients who underwent robot-assisted knee replacement experienced similar levels of pain, mobility, and recovery to those who received conventional surgery. The findings provide important evidence about the use of robotics in health care and highlight where future technological developments and research could make a difference. Coordinated by the University of Warwick and University Hospitals Coventry and Warwickshire (UHCW) NHS Trust, the trial was published in The Lancet, the world's oldest and one of its best-known general medical journals.

Industry observers note that robotic technology is becoming increasingly common in knee replacement surgery around the world. It is now used in 6% of procedures in the UK, 16% in the US, and 42% in Australia. The technology is designed to help surgeons position artificial knee joints more accurately and customize procedures to suit each patient's anatomy.

The UK-wide RACER-Knee trial was funded by the National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR) in partnership with Stryker, the manufacturer of the robotic equipment evaluated in the study. The Warwick Clinical Trials Unit, UHCW NHS Trust, and the Royal Orthopaedic Hospital in Birmingham led the research. It represents the world's largest double-blinded, randomized controlled trial comparing traditional total knee replacement with procedures performed using the Stryker Mako robotic system, the most widely used system of its kind worldwide.

Greater Precision Does Not Improve Recovery.

Industry observers note that twelve months after surgery, patients in both groups reported comparable recovery, mobility, and pain levels. Although the robotic system enabled surgeons to operate with greater precision, patients did not experience measurable improvements in their overall outcomes during the first year. The researchers also found no increased risk of serious adverse events associated with robotic assistance, suggesting that it was as safe as conventional surgery.

The trial was jointly led by two chief investigators in the UK.

Industry observers note that professor Andrew Metcalfe, of Warwick Medical School at the University of Warwick and a consultant orthopedic surgeon at UHCW NHS Trust, remarked: "We are delighted to have completed this world-leading randomized trial of an exciting technology that is now being used globally and at scale. It is an vital step in the process of innovation and will stimulate lots more high-quality studies. We are very grateful for the support of the many patients who took part which is so important, but also the NIHR and Stryker for working so well together to support this critical study. Technology such as this could really help the care we give for patients, but for robotic-assisted knee replacements, there is still work to do before we see benefits such as less pain or better movement.".

Professor Edward Davis, a consultant orthopedic surgeon at The Royal Orthopaedic Hospital NHS Foundation Trust and honorary professor at the University of Birmingham, noted: "The trial demonstrates robotic-arm-assistance allows for higher precision, and in theory the system should allow surgeons to customize the procedure according to a patient's anatomy. These results are by no means a condemnation of the robotic systems, but more understanding of the ideal position for a knee replacement and personalization for each patient is needed. We'll then be able to truly take advantage of the advanced precision of robotic systems.".

Industry observers note that professor Anthony Gordon, director of the NIHR Health Technology Assessment (HTA) Programme, remarked: "Innovation in healthcare depends on evaluating promising technologies rigorously and at scale. While this study reveals robotic-assisted knee replacement is not yet improving patient outcomes, it highlights opportunities to refine these technologies and harness their precision to deliver better care in the future. The NIHR continues to fund robust studies, such as RACER, ensuring we learn how to deliver the latest technologies most effectively within the NHS.".

How Robotic Knee Replacement Works.

Industry observers note that total knee replacement is among the most frequently performed elective surgical procedures worldwide for people with knee arthritis. During traditional surgery, orthopedic surgeons use standard surgical instruments and rely on their training and experience to position the artificial joint.

In a recent development, robotic technology offers an alternative approach in which the surgeon controls a robotic arm during the operation. The system helps position surgical instruments with exceptional accuracy and allows surgeons to adjust the angles and depths of their cuts with greater flexibility. These capabilities make it possible to customize procedures to individual anatomy in ways that are not achievable with conventional techniques.

Landmark Trial Finds Similar Patient Outcomes.

The study involved 339 patients treated by 33 surgeons at 10 hospitals across the UK. Despite the potential advantages of robotic technology, researchers found no meaningful difference between the two groups in the trial's primary outcome measure, the Forgotten Joint Score, one year after surgery.

This assessment measures how conscious patients are of their artificial joint while carrying out everyday activities. Ideally, a successful knee replacement allows patients to go about their daily lives without frequently noticing the artificial joint. Patients achieved similar scores regardless of which surgical technique was used.

Other measures also showed comparable results. These included walking ability, pain during hospitalization, pain during the first three months of recovery and at 12 months, and the likelihood of requiring another operation.

Researchers blueprint to monitor participants for ten years to determine whether differences between the two surgical approaches emerge over a longer period. One particularly vital question is whether robotic assistance reduces the number of patients who eventually need additional knee surgery.

Robotic Knee Surgery Takes Longer and Costs More.

Operations performed with robotic assistance required additional time (on average 10.5 minutes) and cost approximately £950 more per procedure.

Although the robotic system improved surgical precision, it was not associated with a higher risk of serious adverse events, indicating that the procedure appeared to be as safe as traditional knee replacement.

However, when assessed against current NHS spending thresholds, the robotic technology evaluated in the trial was not considered cost-effective during the first year following surgery.

The Future of Personalized Knee Replacement.

The researchers believe that robotic technology could become more valuable if surgeons learn how to use its enhanced precision to better accommodate differences in individual patients' anatomy.

According to recent reports, determining the ideal placement of an artificial knee joint for each patient could eventually allow surgeons to turn greater technical accuracy into meaningful improvements in recovery, pain relief, and mobility. Achieving those benefits will require further technological development and additional research, making personalized robotic surgery a promising area for future investigation.

The findings of the RACER-Knee trial were published in The Lancet.

In a recent development, the research was organized by University Hospitals Coventry and Warwickshire NHS Trust and the University of Warwick. Funding was provided by the UK NHS research organization, the National Institute for Health Research, through its Health Technology Assessment Programme (NIHR128768).

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mega Man: Dual Override’s 2025 reveal brought back the classic boss design contest, asking fans to create and submit their own robot masters, with Capcom choosing one to include in the game. After thousands of submissions, we have our winner; meet Cleanser Man.

As his name suggests, Cleanser Man is a cleaning robot who attacks (and tidies) using a long, multi-cleaning hose arm. Capcom has provided the following character summary:.

Cleanser Man is a cleaning robot with an obsession for pristine beauty. Fueled by an extremely sensitive dirt sensor, Cleaner Man’s ideal world is one without a speck of dust. However, his devotion to cleanliness has a cost. His aggressive scrubbing causes great damage to global landmarks and historic works of art. This fixation has caused the public to view him as more of a threat than a helping hand. Furious and feeling misunderstood, Cleanser Man seizes control of trash processing facility and uses it to pollute the environment with hopes of forcing the world to appreciate the importance of cleanliness.

Cleanser Man won out among the six finalists, a few of which were also cleaning-themed bosses. “In the end, we chose Cleanser Man because of the unique way the concept was brought together and the originality of the color design,” says game director Shinya Ikuta. “While staying true to and respecting the original submission, we adjusted certain details to better fit the world and style of the game.”  Unfortunately, Capcom has not revealed Cleanser Man's creator, but you can see the character in action in the reveal video below.

Industry observers note that in addition to Cleanser Man, Mega Man: Dual Override's rogues' gallery includes the following revealed robot masters: Twinkle Girl, Jet Man, Tank Man, and Cook Man. The remaining three bosses have yet to be revealed.

Mega Man: Dual Override rolls out in 2027 for PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X/S, Switch 2, PlayStation 4, Xbox One, Switch, and PC. To learn more about the game, read our extended preview here. You can also check out the game's recently revealed amiibo figures for the Switch versions.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Though it may seem like we just had a big life sim release in Heartopia, 2026 actually has more than one highly-anticipated release in that particular subgenre of cozy game. The next big one on the horizon is Starsand Island, the life and farming sim from Seed Sparkle Lab.

The game has been gaining momentum since the launch of a demo in October last year, but the developer never quite managed to commit to a date for its debut title. Until now.

Seed Sparkle Lab revealed today that Starsand Island will enter Early Access on February 11, which is only a bit over one week from now. This goes for Steam and the Xbox Preview Program version.

In a recent development, the developer said to expect a fairly short Early Access run, as the full launch is expected in the summer of this year. When the full release arrives, the game will also make the jump to PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series, as well as Switch 2.

The full release is also expected to bring Steam Deck support and introduce the multiplayer mode, which will not be available during Early Access.

Starsand Island has something of a unique look compared to other games in the subgenre. The storybook, anime-inspired aesthetics are popular in the realm of gacha games, of course. However, seeing as this particular game isn’t gacha, being a premium product means it’s going to offer something free-to-play games aren’t designed to.

It has been revealed that speaking of which, the game will be available in two editions: Standard and Deluxe, with the latter including Romanticism-inspired outfits, furniture, and other customisation items. If you buy either during launch, you’ll also get a Chinese New Year bonus with even more outfits and furniture.

On top of the usual systems of farming, mining, and making friends with adorable characters (and animals), the game also has combat that pits you against ancient guardians. You can, of course, also build a home in it, and decorate it to your heart's content.

Seed Sparkle Lab says you can expect about 100 hours of content in the Early Access launch build, and more features will arrive over the course of the next six or so months, including a crossover event with My Time At Portia.

In a recent development, you can look forward to more Starsand Island coverage from us in the near future. Until then, you can get started by planning who you’re going to date now.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that shopify Rebellion Black opened the North America Qualifier Playoffs with a 2-0 win over Xora Esports. The non-partner organisation is now one win from the playoffs that decide a guaranteed São Paulo Kickoff place.

The best-of-three Group Stage meeting with Xora began at 00:10 UTC on Saturday 21 November, opening Shopify Rebellion Black’s VCT Americas Kickoff: North America 2027 campaign.

The result counts for more because Shopify Rebellion is now outside Riot’s partnership system. The organisation was one of the Americas sides that said it had not been chosen for the 2027-2028 partnership programme, Sheep Esports reported. Cloud9, ENVY, M80, FlyQuest and LYON were also on that list. Riot now has eight partner teams in each of its four regions.

The Swiss Stage runs from 20 to 22 November 2026. Every match is best of three. Two wins send a team through to the playoffs, and two losses knock it out. The eight teams left after the Swiss phase move into a double-elimination bracket played over six competition days, with the playoffs set for 1 to 6 December. The event is listed as an online, A-Tier Riot Games qualifier for 16 teams.

Shopify Rebellion Black’s next opponents are Oafs, who also won their opening match 2-0, against QoR. Both teams are therefore one win from the playoffs. Oafs already have a record against Xora. They knocked them out of the Qualifier 1 bracket on 8 November with a 2-1 win. Xora had still reached the Qualifier Playoffs by finishing joint third in the 512-team North America Qualifier 1.

It has been revealed that across 83 rated matches, Shopify Rebellion Black hold a 59-24 record. Before this event their most recent series was a 2-3 defeat to 2GAME Esports at the VCL Americas Last Chance Qualifier 2026. Earlier in that event they had beaten 2GAME Esports 2-1 and Contra 2-0.

The organisation’s second line-up had a harder start. Shopify Rebellion Gold lost 0-2 to Maryville University. Several of the other organisations left out of the partnership programme won their first matches. Cloud9 beat counterfeit 2-0, Team Envy beat Yellow Dragon Gaming 2-0 and FlyQuest edged Masterclass 2-1. Elsewhere, Winthrop University beat SaD Esports 2-0 and YFP Gaming beat Wildcard 2-1.

It has been revealed that the prize for coming through the bracket is a place in São Paulo. Riot will stage the 2027 VCT Americas Kickoff in Brazil. Its eight Partner Teams get direct entry. Non-partner teams can win four places: one guaranteed slot each for North America, Brazil and Latin America, plus one for the Americas Last Chance Qualifier. For a non-partner side, a later run to Masters would be worth a fixed US$200,000 and a place at Champions US$400,000, Dot Esports reported. The regional Kickoff events are due to start on 14 January 2027 and run until 7 February 2027.

I'm not saying Sleeping Dogs is the world's best life of crime sim, but no other game has replicated the importance of pork buns to whole manhood as deftly

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1271 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rockpapershotgun

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For absolutely no reason whatsoever, I’ve recently fired Sleeping Dogs up again.
  • Tonally and in terms of setting, Sleeping Dogs feels a lot closer to GTA 4’s gritty urban gangland drama than Rockstar’s follow-up did.
  • For Wei, it’s a balancing act between his day-to-day life surviving among the triads, and keeping his hands clean while securing evidence against them as an undercover cop.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For absolutely no reason whatsoever, I’ve recently fired Sleeping Dogs up again. The United Front Games-developed, Square Enix-published open-world crime romp is still as good as it’s always been, and still occupies its own corner in the dingy bar where the GTAs and GTA-likes hang out. Back in 2015, RPS co-founderman Alec Meer (RPS in peace) referred to it as “the halfway house between GTA's sneering arrogance and Saints Row's chaotic nonchalance”. Fair enough, I’ve never been that substantial a Saints Row guy, but I see slumbering canines a bit differently.

Tonally and in terms of setting, Sleeping Dogs feels a lot closer to GTA 4’s gritty urban gangland drama than Rockstar’s follow-up did. GTA 5 is an exotic and sun-kissed heist movie, a mould that GTA 6’s tale of gun-toting love in Vice City very much looks to follow. That leaves Sleeping Dogs protagonist Wei Shen standing next to Niko Bellic. One might be kicking faces in Hong Kong and the other might be getting into shootouts in New York, but both are fresh off the boat in places both familiar and alien. They find themselves caught between two lives.

For Wei, it’s a balancing act between his day-to-day life surviving among the triads, and keeping his hands clean while securing evidence against them as an undercover cop. For Niko, it’s a balancing act between trying to settle old scores and start a fresh life in post 9/11 America. One can stop at a street vendor to buy a pork bun to chow down on. One can stop at a street vendor to buy a hotdog to chow down on. Both of their games are beloved for delivering tales which get the player invested in Wei and Niko specifically, that excel in putting you into the emotional shoes of these two underworld operators whose worlds are tearing at them from multiple angles as they claw their way to the top of the food chain.

Despite my headline gag, they do this with a comparably minimal amount of in-depth life-simmy details, like those that’re baked into Red Dead Redemption 2 (and GTA 6, to a degree) as some of the main selling points. Wei can buy a pork bun, the vendor loudly informs him that by doing so he’s avoiding the possibility of never becoming a whole man, but there’s no ‘whole manliness’ meter which demands to be satiated with regular pork bun munching, lest Wei become a less than whole man. All it does is give him a temporary health regeneration boost, because as we all know, the first thing the doctors do if you’re admitted to hospital with grievous wounds after a fight is serve you a scrumptious meal that miraculously closes up your cuts in minutes.

In a recent development, sleeping Dogs dedicates all of its life simming effort to making you feel the weight of Wei’s torment as he grapples with an unsustainable double life of sinning and saintly acts. Like GTA 4, it’s not got the time, tech, or budget to adorn itself with animations or systems that replicate every aspect of Wei’s day-to-day existence in excruciating detail. It’s simply assumed, rather than demonstrated, that some of the back alleys he wanders down to bust drug dealers probably smell a bit unpleasant. He doesn’t have over 60 species of bird to catalogue as he commutes from North Point to the businessman-infested Central district, then on to the houseboat-heavy Aberdeen and gated communities of Kennedy Town. Though, he does keep nicking jade statues, in order to persuade his kung fu instructor to teach him some fun new ways to knee baddies into submission.

He can sing his lungs out to nail I Fought the Law at one of Hong Kong’s few karaoke booths or lose all of his cash playing mahjong, but he doesn’t have an endless laundry list of optional hobbies long enough to suck players who aren’t even particularly trying to get distracted in for hundreds of hours.

Industry observers note that then again, if he wanders into his Central apartment, Wei can take a piss. In truth, I’d forgotten about this prior to my recent revisit, but it is a wonderfully simple feature that really emphasises how things’ve changed for games like these in the years since 2012. I press one button when the prompt pops up near the loo, and Wei unzips before dribbling a rather loud trickle into the bowl. Then, he’s done. I can get him to wash his hands if I wish, but no bladder meter has gone down and no dirtiness meter is being satiated by my scrubbing. If Wei doesn’t take regular whizzes, no NPCs comment that he’s looking a bit pained, and his walking animation doesn’t dynamically adjust to huddle his legs closer together.

You could ask what was even the point of animating Wei’s pissing if it’s a pointless and totally optional activity, outside of arguably doing a tiny bit of work in helping Shen be convincingly human (and it unquestionably being quite funny the first time you stumble across it). By looping what would once have been one-note button presses into systems that help them play a more active role in fleshing out the world and the routines of its inhabitants, uber-detailed games like GTA 6 - at their best - add an extra layer of definition to the tales and adventures they depict.

They often feel like the sort of game Sleeping Dogs might’ve been if it’d had their tech and its budget was the GDP of real world Hong Kong. The question is, when limitations like that don’t apply to the degree they once did, where the line lies between extra layers which tangibly deepen the player’s experience and overindulgent bloat?

Sleeping Dogs, despite working in its own takes on elements of GTA, Saints Row, and I’d argue RGG Studio’s earlier Like A Dragon/Yakuza entries, is an unquestionably lean and focused game. Less isn’t necessarily more, especially if you were to ask slumbering canines-loving teenage me, who would’ve bitten your hand off for Hong Kong to boast even a third of the extra features and activities GTA 6 and Red Dead 2 pack into their life of crime sims.

In a recent development, the latter two are games that wouldn’t have been possible to make, at least in a format the masses would be able to play, back in the era when Sleeping Dogs and GTA 4 represented what an open-world crime game typically looked like. They’ve eaten up what used to be the domain of arcade racers like Midnight Club and hunting sims to step closer to being something reminiscent of Better Than Life, the addictive VR everything game from the Red Dwarfverse, which takes over players’ lives by simulating a world where everything they want can play out in reality-mimicking detail.

They aim to be far, far more than what defined their predecessors, and to use that to appeal to an ever-expanding audience. What I’m intrigued to see, whenever I get my hands on Rockstar’s latest work, is whether those like me who come to it having recently played a game like Sleeping Dogs will find a game that feels like it’s being pulled in a million different directions, to the point that it loses something of what historically has been at the centre of its fundamental appeal.

Or, to put it another way: is there a point at which you’ve eaten so many pork buns in one sitting that you begin to stray away from the self-actualisation which steady consumption of them is known to facilitate?

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Pocket monsters, just not those ones.

According to recent reports, pre-registration only opened at the end of October, so Bandai hasn't kept anyone waiting long. Digimon Alysion is out now on iOS and Android, finally putting the Digimon Card Game on your phone.

Expect an original story with a brand latest cast of characters, plus a few Digimon you won't have come across before. It's built to teach you the rules as you play through it. The tutorial covers how cards are laid out and used, along with the basics of a battle.

Your collection mixes cards from the physical Digimon Card Game with latest ones made for Alysion. On top of that, you’ve got Shiny Cards, Alt-Art Cards and Premium Alt-Art Cards (the animated ones), and you'll get one free pack a day to build your decks from.

Once you’ve fleshed out your kit, you can take it into ranked against people from around the world, or keep things relaxed and spar against friends and characters from the story instead. Breeding is back as well, for that matter. You can raise Digimon and Digivolve them all the way up to Mega, and there's a Digidex of more than 100 entries to fill in.

According to recent reports, pokémon TCG Pocket is the obvious comparison, and probably the reason Digimon Alysion is arriving now at all. The difference is that Bandai isn't starting from scratch, and if you've been playing the physical version, you'll recognise a fair bit of what’s part of your packs.

Bandai has already done something similar with Dragon Ball's Fusion World, which you can play digitally and on paper, so it's a fairly safe bet the game is meant to send some people towards the physical cards too.

Digimon Alysion is free-to-play with in-app purchases on the App Store and Google Play, and a launch event, Battle Carnival Dukemon Ver., is running now.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Industry observers note that bruce Nesmith, a long-time developer at Bethesda who worked on Skyrim and the Fallout games (including as a quest designer on Fallout 3), explained the atmosphere back in the mid-to-late 2000s to The Examined Game.
  • According to recent reports, "There were a lot of people who were Obsidian fans who were like, 'Bethesda's going to screw it up, they're just going to make it [Oblivion], we want Fallout the way we remember Fallout, these guys should never have had it,'" he notes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It might be hard to believe now, but Bethesda wasn't everyone's top choice for bringing back the Fallout series. In fact, when it came to Fallout 3, Obsidian was the studio many fans wanted to see tackle the wasteland, emboldening the team behind The Elder Scrolls to get things right for the sci-fi RPG.

Industry observers note that bruce Nesmith, a long-time developer at Bethesda who worked on Skyrim and the Fallout games (including as a quest designer on Fallout 3), explained the atmosphere back in the mid-to-late 2000s to The Examined Game. "There was huge pushback when Bethesda got the Fallout license to do Fallout 3," he remembers.

According to recent reports, "There were a lot of people who were Obsidian fans who were like, 'Bethesda's going to screw it up, they're just going to make it [Oblivion], we want Fallout the way we remember Fallout, these guys should never have had it,'" he notes. "There was a strong vocal community that just hated that we were going to make that game.".

According to recent reports, if you can cast your mind back to the era, Obsidian would've seemed like a more appealing choice. Knights of the Old Republic 2: The Sith Lords in 2004 proved the team's ability to handle sprawling science-fiction, and Bethesda's push into open-world design didn't quite blend with the nuance of the early Fallout releases.

But Todd Howard and his crew weren't about to let the doubters win. If anything, they became more dedicated to making Fallout 3. "We had to prove them wrong," Nesmith claims. "And fortunately, we did. And Fallout 3 was embraced, even by a lot of our skeptics.".

It has been revealed that he mentions there was a portion of the fanbase who maintain that Fallout 2 was the franchise highlight, and will forever remain so. "But we tried our best to just not engage. You're not going to win that argument, you're not going to persuade hearts and minds," he adds. "All you can do is make the best game you can make and let that be your statement.".

Industry observers note that and Fallout 3 is quite the statement. Obsidian did give us Fallout: Newly introduced Vegas in 2010, and then we got Fallout 4 from Bethesda in 2015. When will we see Fallout 5? That's anyone's guess, but Obsidian is apparently working on another game set in the wasteland for the time-being.

  • As is often the case, what stands out most about these nominees is how, generally speaking, they don't fully align with gaming culture's favorite soundtracks of the year, and instead often trend toward the most recognizable IP (often franchises with films) of the year.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Since 2023, the Recording Academy has included an official category for video game soundtracks, adding an air of legitimacy to a diverse musical medium we know and love. Today, we learned the list of nominees for the 2027 Grammy ceremony, and it's an interesting lineup. The nominations are as follows:.

As is often the case, what stands out most about these nominees is how, generally speaking, they don't fully align with gaming culture's favorite soundtracks of the year, and instead often trend toward the most recognizable IP (often franchises with films) of the year. On that note, it's most surprising to see that Avatar: Frontiers of Pandora has been nominated for the third year in a row: once for the base game, once for the Secrets of the Spires DLC, and now for the From The Ashes DLC. None of these soundtracks are bad by any means, but their Grammy representation far outweighs their cultural footprint.

It has been revealed that the standout here is Ghost of Yōtei, which is not an adaptation of the massive franchises the other games fall into. However, it's also a Sony-published game, which have a pretty good track record of getting nominations, potentially due to the company's massive presence in the music and film industries. Still, Ghost of Yōtei has a great, unique score that's deserving of its spot, and also one previously nominated for best music at the 2025 Game Awards. The Grammys accept any releases between October 1 of one year and September 30 of the following year, so Ghost of Yōtei barely made the cut for this window. The Game Awards nominees will be declared tomorrow – it will be interesting to see how much overlap there is between the categories.

This batch of Grammy noms also has fewer recurring nominees than past years. This is Gordy Haab's third nomination (he won in 2024 for Star Wars Jedi: Survivor) and John Paesano's second nomination (he was nominated in 2025 for Marvel's Spider-Man 2). It's also the first year since the awards' creation without Bear McCreary or Austin Wintory nominations.

Industry observers note that last year's nominations left a sour taste in the mouths of many, with several DLC nominees and a complete lack of Clair Obscur: Expedition 33, the year's standout hit that many specifically praised for its music. This year certainly has snubs (Mewgenics, Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave, and Control Resonant all come to mind), but none as egregious as last year.

#155325. The Most Loved and Hated JRPGs by Fans

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1616 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dualshockers ↗ Open Full Page

The Most Loved and Hated JRPGs by Fans

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1616 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dualshockers

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that JRPGs have long since become a distinct phenomenon as a specific subgenre of RPGs, even when they are not produced in Japan.
  • However, while there is a slightly more civilized consensus around what makes the best fighting game or racing game, the JRPGs fanbase always seems deeply divided.
  • I will alternate between hated and loved entries and avoid repeating franchises to keep the list dynamic.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that JRPGs have long since become a distinct phenomenon as a specific subgenre of RPGs, even when they are not produced in Japan. Fixed characters, linear narratives, creative progression, and an atduesthetic usually inspired by anime are what tell us at a glance what makes a JRPG stand apart from any other subgenre under the role-playing umbrella. And to be honest, those exact elements are what draw me to the genre, sometimes removing one or adding another.

However, while there is a slightly more civilized consensus around what makes the best fighting game or racing game, the JRPGs fanbase always seems deeply divided. Some titles seem to sit at the same level of love and hate for fans, no matter which side you're on. That is why I decided to talk today about the most loved and most hated JRPGs by the public. This isn't a consensus or an objective truth, but a fun look at what I have observed after years on forums, debating with fellow JRPG lovers, and tracking the fanbase's overall perception.

I will alternate between hated and loved entries and avoid repeating franchises to keep the list dynamic.

Industry observers note that while I couldn't find a direct primary source confirming this claim, outlets like Kotaku and RPGFan say the same thing: due to Xenosaga Episode II flopping so hard, the series was cut from its intended six episodes to just three. For fans hoping to see Tetsuya Takahashi's vision fully realized, that was a massive blow and certainly left a mark of hatred on the second Xenosaga.

Recent findings suggest that while Xenosaga Episode I: Der Wille zur Macht went over budget and featured far more cinematics than the average JRPG player was accustomed to (yeap), it was still a satisfactory experience. The second one? Not so much. The shift in art direction and the battle system genuinely pushed players away and, allegedly, led Bandai Namco to safeguard its investment by wrapping up the entire story as a trilogy. Much like Xenogears, Xenosaga became a beautiful what-could-have-been scenario, though luckily we eventually got to see Takahashi's ambitions realized with Xenoblade, which is still going strong.

To be completely honest, I am not that big of a fan of EarthBound. I played EarthBound Beginnings, also known as Mother, and found it impressive for an NES JRPG. Shortly after, I moved on to EarthBound, which I had played a long time ago and didn't remember much, and I walked away unimpressed. Maybe the American parody didn't resonate with me (I am not American), or maybe I played it too late, and the cultural zeitgeist didn't hit me the same way.

Sources indicate that even so, I fully recognize how much people who enjoy this JRPG truly adore it. They spare no praise, speak fondly of the experience, and admire not only the game itself, but also its creator, Shigesato Itoi. Many of those fans claim Mother 3, a title that never officially left Japan, is even better, but since I didn't vibe with the second entry, I have little interest in trying it.

Sometimes a game is hated for its themes, other times for an overly boring battle system, or perhaps because of an obnoxious character we cannot stand looking at. Occasionally, however, games draw hatred simply for feeling apathetic, failing to spark any real emotion in the player, and offering nothing particularly remarkable. That's exactly the case with Tales of Zestiria for many Tales fans.

According to recent reports, mind you, I actually enjoy the game, and it was the very first Tales of title where I earned the platinum trophy. I was never overly critical of Sorey's journey, the complex equipment fusion system, or even the misleading marketing around Alisha's protagonism. I mean, okay, fair enough, those all sound like completely valid points of criticism, yet I still had a good time. Not everyone can say the same, and whenever you look at a Tales of tier list, Zestiria almost always sits right at the bottom.

It has been revealed that apparently, there are two types of fans in the JRPG world: those who love Suikoden II and those who haven't played it yet. I am not kidding here. I considered adding Xenogears to this spot because I know it has a very vocal fanbase, quite scary to be honest, borderline toxic. But Suikoden? That feels like a genuine relationship, a true love situation. Every time you meet someone who indicates Suikoden II is their favorite game, you can practically see their eyes light up.

To a large extent, I get it! Suikoden II is awesome. The grounded political plot stood out at a time when countless games were mostly about slaying God in a high fantasy setting. The 108 recruitable characters, each carrying their own motivation and reason for joining the resistance. The six-party-member battles with combo skills, and so on. Okay, you might need to use a walkthrough to recruit everyone and unlock the true ending, but the journey itself is already wonderful, and Luca Blight is a terrific villain. What is there not to love, right? Glory to Suikoden.

Recent findings suggest that there is nothing more miserable than watching a series you love, follow closely, and appreciate in every detail slowly fall from grace. For me, that didn't happen with Star Ocean, because I genuinely love Star Ocean: The Divine Force, though that is precisely how many felt after Star Ocean: Till the End of Time, the third entry. Plenty of fans didn't care for Star Ocean: The Last Hope yet could still stomach it, but Star Ocean: Integrity and Faithlessness? Just mentioning the name makes me feel your glare.

In a recent development, the fifth Star Ocean suffered from an affliction that hit many JRPG franchises during that era: constricting budgets. I know that doesn't excuse its final quality, but it is the reality. The game severely lacked traditional cutscenes, playing out almost entirely through real-time in-engine camera angles, not out of artistic charm, but due to a lack of investment. I still like the game for two reasons: Item Creation remains incredible, and as someone who loves constantly swapping between party members, being able to deploy everyone into battle at once was a blast, even if having seven party members acting simultaneously got confusing and felt like a bit too much. It had a chaotic family reunion vibe, you know.

Out of all the JRPG fans I know, well over half say they discovered or fell in love with the genre after playing Final Fantasy VII. That fact alone could summarize this entire entry, because you either know someone just like that or you are that person yourself. I am a bit older, so I played other JRPGs before FFVII, though my cousin fits that exact mold, since he still uses an email address with the game's acronym in his handle to this day.

It is completely understandable, mind you. Final Fantasy VII was a global phenomenon that paved the way for JRPGs to gain worldwide recognition. That is why if you watch footage from the E3 showcase where the remake was unveiled, you will see countless explosive reactions. I know many newcomers to the genre or franchise don't understand why Square Enix split the remake into three parts, calling the firm mercenary (fitting for the game's plot, to be honest). Yet, I believe Square did it to honor the franchise's legacy, deliver something fresh for longtime fans, and naturally attract a new audience who can experience that same magic veterans felt when they first played and fell in love with it.

Whereas with most entries I listed as most hated (not hated by me, remember!) I tried to soften the blow and use euphemisms to avoid insulting people who enjoy those games or the developers behind them. For Lunar: Dragon Song, though, the gloves are completely off. I had only heard rumors about it, about how this mechanic was terrible and that feature was lousy, until one day I decided to test it for myself.

Good lord, it is awful. So many baffling design decisions make me genuinely wonder how anyone let them pass. First, and most obviously, simply running in the game drains your HP. I mean, what? Then there are two separate reward modes per battle, one granting only experience points and another granting only loot. I didn't understand that system at first and left loot mode active, feeling bizarrely weak despite fighting endless battles. On top of that, combat has mandatory auto-targeting, plus a bland story, forgettable characters, and other uninspiring features. Lunar: Dragon Song is universally hated, and it deserves every bit of it.

Whenever someone asks me which JRPG I would recommend to a complete newcomer to the genre, the answer nine times out of ten is Chrono Trigger. Pointing to a 1995 release even today speaks volumes about the work's enduring relevance and timelessness. And I will go a step further: that recommendation doesn't rely on cheap nostalgia alone, because Chrono Trigger truly is a spectacle, with pacing, gameplay, and design that can captivate even the most stubborn skeptics who resist JRPGs.

And of course, among JRPG enthusiasts, it is tough to find anyone who doesn't genuinely love Chrono Trigger. You might have critiques about it (I certainly do), or complain about one small detail or another. Still, it's nearly impossible to deny that it is a masterpiece and a majestic blueprint for building a JRPG. It stands undeniably as the most beloved JRPG of all time, even if you don't happen to be one of the people who love it.

Loneliness is making us sick, but we may be treating it all wrong

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (719 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that research has established that loneliness can have serious consequences for physical health.
  • Published in Social Problems, the study examines how chronic loneliness and social isolation became recognized as major public health concerns after researchers uncovered links to illness, premature death, and increased healthcare spending.
  • Previous studies highlighted in the research illustrate the severity of these consequences.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that research has established that loneliness can have serious consequences for physical health. However, a latest University of Michigan study warns that treating loneliness primarily as a health problem could shift responsibility away from society and place it on a healthcare system that lacks the tools to restore meaningful social connections.

Published in Social Problems, the study examines how chronic loneliness and social isolation became recognized as major public health concerns after researchers uncovered links to illness, premature death, and increased healthcare spending.

Previous studies highlighted in the research illustrate the severity of these consequences. One estimated that lacking social connections could be as harmful to health as smoking 15 cigarettes a day. Another found that loneliness, social isolation, and living alone were each associated with an approximately 30% higher risk of premature death. The financial burden is also substantial, with separate research estimating that social isolation costs Medicare $6.7 billion each year in care for older adults.

Sources indicate that "Once people saw these findings, they began to treat loneliness as urgent," said University of Michigan doctoral student Sofia Hiltner. "But it made me wonder: Why do we only consider problems vital once they are tied to health?".

The Problem With Medicalizing Loneliness.

To understand how loneliness became a medical concern, Hiltner conducted interviews with experts and reviewed more than a decade of media coverage, medical journal articles, and academic literature.

According to recent reports, her analysis revealed that establishing a connection between loneliness and poor health helped the problem gain credibility. However, it also encouraged what she describes as a "logical leap": the belief that any problem affecting human health should become the responsibility of the healthcare system.

It has been revealed that "Not everything that relates to health belongs in healthcare," she said. "Doctors can screen patients and connect them to services, but they cannot rebuild communities or shorten work hours.".

Hiltner, a predoctoral trainee in social demography at the Population Studies Center within the University of Michigan's Institute for Social Research, was inspired to investigate loneliness after witnessing her grandmother become increasingly isolated as she aged.

When Hiltner entered graduate school to research social isolation among older adults, she learned that clinical trials were investigating a "loneliness pill." The discovery prompted her to question why loneliness was being approached primarily as a medical condition rather than a social problem.

"After my grandfather died, my grandmother lived alone and there was little structure in her life," Hiltner mentioned. "She didn't seem to have many friends or activities. It made me think about everything that happened throughout her life that led to that point. I wondered about the social policies, in addition to dynamics at the family level, that could have helped prevent that situation.".

Finding Solutions Beyond the Healthcare System.

Interestingly, Hiltner found that the medical community was initially reluctant to take responsibility for addressing loneliness. Much of the momentum behind incorporating loneliness into healthcare instead came from academic researchers, government health officials, and insurance companies.

Although recognizing loneliness as a medical concern can generate greater awareness and encourage intervention, it may also divert valuable resources from efforts to address the social circumstances that leave people isolated.

Industry observers note that "There is the risk that defining loneliness as medical crowds out other ways of responding to the issue," she said. "Attention, time and resources are limited. On the other hand, framing it as medical may inspire more action than would have otherwise happened.".

Hiltner hopes her findings will encourage policymakers to reconsider how they define social problems and explore preventive strategies that address their underlying causes before they develop into serious health concerns.

"I would like them to reflect on the strengths and limitations of addressing problems through the healthcare system, and look farther upstream to understand how a problem emerges, considering ways to intervene before it occurs," she remarked. "Healthcare can help, but it can only go so far.".

Sources indicate that it sounds like Koei Tecmo’s decision to finally release a Nioh game on PC day-and-date with PlayStation has paid off. The highly-anticipated Nioh 3 has gone live across both platforms, a first for a series that typically spends its initial release months as a console exclusive.

On Steam, and despite having only been available for just a few hours, the game has broken series records, and it continues to climb.

According to recent reports, at the time of writing, Nioh 3 has peaked at 42,822 concurrent players on Steam (via SteamDB), and the number keeps going up. Because it’s in the middle of day in Europe and everyone is at work, it’s entirely possible - if not likely - that this figure will get much higher. A weekend bump is also possible, as we’ve seen with several recent releases.

As it stands, the current peak concurrent is enough to get the game in Steam’s top 20 most played games.

Recent findings suggest that this already puts it ahead of all other Nioh games on Steam. The original Nioh peaked at 10,649 when it released in November, 2017. Nioh 2 fared much better, peaking at 41,325 concurrent players in February, 2021.

Sources indicate that of course, you could see that success coming a mile away. The game is currently number one worldwide in Steam’s list of top sellers. This is a jump of 46 positions, for a total of three weeks Nioh 3 has spent in that list.

There are many reasons as to why Nioh 3 has done as well as it has. Word of mouth coming off last year’s PS5-exclusive demo, and the more positive coverage that followed since are just two.

Just last week, Team Ninja released a pretty generous demo across both platforms, which has been well received by players, and likely contributed to sales, in no small part because progress in the demo carries over to the full game.

In a recent development, critical reviews have been incredibly positive, too. We awarded the game four out of five stars, calling it “Team Ninja’s most accomplished action game, and the series’ most accessible.” It will be interesting to see what number the highest peak concurrent actually settles on over the weekend.

According to recent reports, until then, if you’re jumping in yourself, our Nioh 3 guides are essential reading. Start off with these useful and actually informative gameplay tips, and don’t start playing until you’ve changed these settings. Once you’re ready to get deeper, be sure to read up on how to play co-op with other players, and how to summon AI Acolytes to help you out.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, gloomwood, the Victorian survival horror immersive sim (or, wait, I'm getting reports that we shouldn't call it an immersive sim, apparently) by Dillon Rogers is a game that is quite happily inspired by its predecessors such as Thief, Resident Evil and Dishonored; you could call it 'Thief with guns', if you really wanted to.

According to recent reports, gloomwood, the Victorian survival horror immersive sim (or, wait, I'm getting reports that we shouldn't call it an immersive sim, apparently) by Dillon Rogers is a game that is quite happily inspired by its predecessors such as Thief, Resident Evil and Dishonored; you could call it 'Thief with guns', if you really wanted to. (Sorry, I've just seen that the domain for Gloomwood's site used to be 'residenthievil.com'. Wonderful). Now, that last inspiration has come full circle, as publisher New Blood Interactive's latest update post confirms that the newest member of the team is none other than former Dishonored designer Julien Eveillé.

In addition to his work at Arkane on Dishonored and its sequel, Deathloop, and even Marvel's Blade, Eveillé also developed his own indie horror, 2024's short and sweet Threshold. It's quite a legacy to add to this team, and his hiring is described by Upcoming Blood as an example of how "finding level designers who are up to the task of working on Gloomwood is not easy". The post also mentions that Eveillé will be added alongside "our new devs", implying that he's not the only new addition to the team.

Other than these new hires, the update is set to include quite a bit to change up Gloomwood and make it bigger. The highlight is the First National Bank level, which is described as "our largest and most intricately designed level yet", with the screenshots showing off a grand and imposing, yet claustrophobic in places, that makes the act of going to the bank even more intimidating than usual. The Bank is joined by the new stun prod weapon, which is self-explanatory, and the new Rat and Fishdog transformations, which let you sneak through crawlspaces and swim through dirtied waters respectively. That sneaking will be made more difficult by the addition of alarms and blood pools that both alert surrounding guards to your presence, though the new Crow King transformation offers a new, acid-belching way to take down any guards that come running.

The patch is tentatively scheduled for "before the end of the year", but Upcoming Blood aren't setting down a specific release date. Rogers himself will also be going through back surgery very soon, for which I wish him a gentle recovery and, hopefully, as easy a return to work as possible.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Regular physical activity has long been recognized as a way to help protect against dementia.
  • An analysis involving more than 4.2 million people found that recreational activities such as walking, cycling, running, swimming, and playing sports were associated with a significantly lower risk of dementia.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Regular physical activity has long been recognized as a way to help protect against dementia. However, latest research from the University of Southern California (USC) suggests that the circumstances in which people are physically active may be just as important as the amount of activity they get.

An analysis involving more than 4.2 million people found that recreational activities such as walking, cycling, running, swimming, and playing sports were associated with a significantly lower risk of dementia. Surprisingly, people who engaged in higher levels of physical activity at work appeared to face an increased risk of developing the condition.

Published in The Lancet Public Health, the study is the first systematic investigation into whether a phenomenon known as the "physical activity paradox" also applies to dementia. Already well established in cardiovascular research, this paradox refers to the observation that physical labor does not necessarily offer the same health advantages as recreational exercise and may even be associated with a greater risk of disease.

In a recent development, led by David Raichlen, professor of biological sciences and anthropology at the USC Dornsife College of Letters, Arts and Sciences, the research team examined data from 74 cohort and case-control studies. Together, the studies included more than 4.2 million people between the ages of 45 and 93 from 30 countries. Over a median follow-up period of 10 years, researchers monitored diagnoses of all-cause dementia, Alzheimer's disease, and vascular dementia.

Recent findings suggest that participants who engaged in higher levels of recreational physical activity had a 24% lower risk of dementia compared with the least active individuals. Physical activity associated with household chores also appeared to offer benefits, although this finding was supported by only one study. In contrast, higher levels of physical activity at work were linked to a 20% greater risk of dementia. Physically active commuting was also associated with a modest increase in risk, but evidence for this relationship came from just two studies.

"The findings challenge the long-held assumption that 'every move counts' for brain health," said Natan Feter, the study's first author, a postdoctoral fellow in Raichlen's Evolutionary Biology of Physical Activity Lab at USC and a researcher in the Graduate Program of Epidemiology at Universidade Federal do Rio Grande do Sul (Brazil).

Why Exercise and Physical Labor May Affect the Brain Differently.

Researchers often group recreational exercise, manual labor, household chores, and active commuting together when measuring "Physical activity." However, the authors suggest that the circumstances surrounding these activities vary considerably and could influence their long-term health effects.

Sources indicate that people who exercise during their free time generally have greater control over the intensity and nature of their activities. Recreational exercise can also provide opportunities to socialize and relieve stress. In comparison, physically demanding occupations may require repeated movements, extended periods of standing, heavy lifting, and insufficient time to recover, along with exposure to potentially harmful workplace conditions.

Recent findings suggest that the researchers do not believe that physical movement itself is likely to explain the elevated dementia risk associated with occupational activity. Instead, the relationship may arise from the social and environmental factors commonly associated with manual labor.

Physically demanding occupations are more likely to expose workers to psychological and social stress, limited control over their work, unsafe conditions, and higher levels of air and noise pollution. Each of these factors has independently been associated with dementia risk. Workers may also struggle to participate in recreational exercise because of exhaustion, limited free time, or a lack of access to safe spaces for physical activity.

Opposing Patterns in Dementia Risk.

The researchers also discovered that the relationship between physical activity and dementia risk was not linear and followed opposite patterns depending on the type of activity.

Recent findings suggest that as recreational exercise increased, dementia risk gradually declined until the apparent benefits leveled off. Occupational physical activity demonstrated the reverse pattern, with dementia risk increasing at higher activity levels before eventually reaching a plateau.

Important Limitations and Unanswered Questions.

According to recent reports, the authors emphasize that there is still too little research on physical activity related to household chores and commuting to draw definitive conclusions about either. Most of the available evidence also comes from high-income countries, despite projections that low- and middle-income nations will experience the greatest increases in dementia cases in the coming decades.

According to recent reports, another limitation is that almost all the studies depended on participants reporting their own physical activity. This approach can introduce errors if people do not accurately remember their activity levels. Nevertheless, Feter remarked the consistency of the findings across several additional statistical analyses suggests that the observed relationships warrant serious attention.

Industry observers note that the researchers stress that their findings should not discourage people from pursuing physically active occupations. Since the analysis relied on observational research, it cannot establish that occupational physical activity causes dementia.

Instead, the results underscore the importance of examining the conditions under which people are physically active. Recreational exercise continued to be associated with a lower risk of dementia, while occupational activity remained linked to a higher risk even after researchers accounted for differences in age, education, and chronic health conditions.

How Sedentary Activities May Also Influence Brain Health.

In a recent development, the importance of context may extend beyond physical activity. Separate research by Raichlen, Feter, and their colleagues, published recently in the journal Alzheimer's & Dementia, suggests that different types of sedentary behavior may also be associated with differences in brain structure.

Sources indicate that in that study, mentally stimulating activities performed while sitting, such as working at a desk, were associated with greater volume in certain regions of the cerebral cortex than more passive activities, such as watching television. These differences included brain regions involved in executive function.

Together, the findings could have vital implications for public health strategies aimed at reducing dementia risk. The authors suggest that encouraging people to "move more" may not be sufficient without also addressing the circumstances in which physical activity takes place.

"In other words, when it comes to protecting the brain, the context of physical activity may matter just as much as movement itself," Raichlen remarked. "Improving access to safe parks, walking trails and recreational facilities, ensuring people have adequate leisure time for exercise, and reducing harmful workplace exposures may ultimately prove as key as promoting physical activity itself.".

Raichlen and Feter's co-authors include Tiladia Markarian, Dylan M. Luong, Jack Gunnink, Anamika Nanda, Sarah Hourihan and Ashley Ventura of USC; Eduardo Caputo, Jayne Feter, Gustavo S. Silva and Airton José Rombaldi of Universidade Federal de Pelotas (Brazil); Paula Iso-Markku of the University of Helsinki (Finland); Daniela Benzano Bumaguin of Fundação Universitária de Cardiologia (Brazil); Yann C. Klimentidis and Gene E. Alexander of the University of Arizona; Daniel Umpierre and Natália Schröder of Universidade Federal do Rio Grande do Sul (Brazil); and Pedro C. Hallal of University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign.

Funding for the research included National Institutes of Health grants P30AG072980, P30AG019610, R56AG067200, R01AG064587 and R01AG072445, along with support from the state of Arizona, the Arizona Department of Health Services and the McKnight Brain Research Foundation. Additional financial support was provided in part by the Fundação de Amparo à Pesquisa do Estado do Rio Grande do Sul (FAPERGS) (25/2551-0002834-5) and the National Council for Scientific and Technological Development - CNPq and Department of Science and Technology of Secretariat of Science, Technology, Innovation and Health Complex of Ministry of Health of Brazil - MoH (445538/2023-6).

As we head towards the weekend, it's becoming increasingly cold and dark, and that means you'll probably want to sit and find a mobile game to sink plenty of time into. Well, you're in luck, because there's a constant glut of great fresh releases, including the launch of Dicevaders on iOS!

Dicevaders sees you taking on the role not of defender of the Earth, but of its invaders and destroyers. To do so, you'll need to gradually overwhelm the defences of each of Earth's bastions, and you'll do so with dice (naturally). In essence, you place units, build up multipliers and gradually overcome the defence rating of each planet to destroy it.

According to recent reports, it makes for a rather interesting combination of luck and strategy, where you'll need to think about when you might need to reroll and keep your supply of currencies stocked up to do so. The graphics are, of course, the kind of crunchy, colourful pixels I'm fond of, so you won't hear any complaints from me, and the mix of blues, purples and reds makes for a thoroughly alien colour palette.

There's plenty of synergy, different commanders and units to take advantage of too. So if you're looking for a game with plenty of depth to enjoy this winter, why not check out Dicevaders on iOS?
